From:	phyllis.wilkerson@att.net
Sent:	Wednesday, September 29, 2004 12:19 PM
To:	Jeb Bush
Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Phyllis Wilkerson 404 Royalty Run Place Apt #3 Brandon, FL 33511 United States

From:	Jan Bergemann <janberg@aug.com>
Sent:	Wednesday, April 10, 2002 11:07 AM
To:	Gov. Jeb Bush; Jeb Bush
Subject:	Some serious thoughts

Dear Governor,
I'm writing to you as a registered Republican and a strong supporter of the candidates of your party, not in my other official position as President of CCFJ, Inc., a grass root organization, which had in the last year a more than 400% increase in membership. This is just some food for thought and I hope that you seriously see it as such.
 
When you took office a lot of consumers and homeowners all around the state had hoped for a change of the old system, meaning ignoring the wishes of the constituents. But after two legislative sessions it seems very obvious that nothing has really changed. Since years homeowners' activist from all over the State have politely asked the legislature to consider changes regarding the Statutes of Mandated Properties.
Most of them were stopped by legislators, industry and lobbyists before they left the starting holes.
This year, with the help of some Republican legislators, namely Dean of the House Jerry Melvin, we succeeded with prefiling a proposed Mandated Property Reform Task Force bill  <http://www.ccfj.net/Taskforce.htm> (HB 887 + SB 1484) . This bill found very good support in the House, but some Republican Senators in influential committee positions just let it die in committee, without even giving it the fair chance of a vote. This was an obvious showing of these Senators not being willing to consider consumer friendly legislation. All we had asked for was a Task Force to sit together with the stakeholders to discuss necessary changes in the Statutes and enforcement of such. But not even that seems to be in the interest of the industry partisans, who definitely love the Status Quo, meaning they can't really be held responsible for any wrongdoing.
 
The voices of the constituents in mainly Republican areas were left unheard. There are big arguments in associations for example in the Jacksonville area and in Marion County. A member of the Florida Silver Haired Legislature collected in a very short time more than 2000 signatures in support of improved homeowners' legislation, but was plainly ignored in Tallahassee. A Marion County Senator stated in a town hall meeting that she has to withdraw her support for these bills after being visited by 10 developers. Other Republican Senators just chose to ignore letters and telephone calls in this regards from their constituents.
These are just a very few of the many examples.
 
The House Staff Analysis clearly supported the creation of such Task Force. And the many pending law-suits all over the State would definitely give a financial reason to act in this regards.
 
Many angry homeowners are willing to make this a serious election issue in autumn, something I don't think would be in the interest of you and the Republican Party.  You definitely know about the problems your brother, our President, has with a Senate with a Democratic majority. It surely wouldn't make your job easier. 
In the community I live in many neighbors backed in the last election a democratic House candidate, who had been willing to pledge his support for consumer-friendly homeowners' legislation in our community newsletter, despite the fact that they are mostly Republican voters. Please don't underestimate the fact that many homeowners are not happy with the existing statutes. Even if a lot of them may not be very outspoken, but a mark is quickly made in the wrong box at the ballot, without having to fear retaliation by a developer or some boardmember.
 
I hope we can, in the interest of all of us, avoid a confrontation about this issue come election time. 
 
I will officially approach you in about two weeks to create this Task Force by executive order, as it is in your power. Please consider my above thoughts before making your decision.
 
If you have any questions in this regards, please feel free to contact me. I would be happy to discuss these issues with you at a time of your convenience. Or, if your time allows, we could as well meet in person for an exchange of opinions. 
 
Warm regards
Jan Bergemann
St. Augustine, FL

Everglades Plan to Raze 77 Homes
Compromise Measure to Revive Park After 14-Year Delay

   By Michael Grunwald
         Staff Writer

   Washington Post

   Monday, February 17, 2003; Page A02

http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/articles/A18572-2003Feb16.html

MIAMI, Feb. 16 -- Congress has approved a plan to destroy 77 homes at the edge of Everglades National Park, jump-starting efforts to restore
flows to the ailing River of Grass after 14 years of delay.

The compromise measure to buy out the most flood-prone portion of what is known as the 8.5 Square Mile Area, a tight-knit Cuban American
neighborhood of mango groves and horse pastures, was supported by President Bush and Gov. Jeb Bush (R), as well as by regulators and
environmentalists. Tucked into last week's $397 billion budget bill, it would revive the Modified Water Deliveries Project of 1989, a long-stalled plan
to rehydrate the parched eastern side of the park.

The revival of "Mod Waters" would also help the much larger $8.4 billion Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, the most ambitious
environmental project in history. The law authorizing the overall Everglades restoration in 2000 specified that several key elements could not
proceed until Mod Waters is complete.

"The logjam is broken," said Sen. Bob Graham (D-Fla.), the original sponsor of Mod Waters as well as the new measure to get it moving. Sen.
George Voinovich (R-Ohio) and Rep. E. Clay Shaw Jr. (R-Fla.) also helped push the buyout, overcoming property-rights opposition from Sen.
James M. Inhofe (R-Okla.) and Rep. Don Young (R-Alaska).

Environmentalists had pushed for a buyout of the entire 8.5 Square Mile Area, but most were happy with the compromise, which is to buy out 44
percent of the land and 12 percent of the homes. The residents of the area, however, were furious, even though their congressman, Rep. Mario
Diaz-Balart (R-Fla.), attached language requiring the Army Corps of Engineers to offer owners of the 77 affected homes land elsewhere in the
neighborhood.

Today, the residents held a protest rally in Miami's Little Havana neighborhood, accusing Jeb Bush of turning his back on Cuban American
supporters. They carried signs, in English and Spanish, vowing: We will not sell.

"This is a shameful travesty," said Alice Pena, president of the local homeowners group. "We're going to keep fighting."

The one bright side, Pena said, was the language assuring the residents a chance to stay in the 8.5 Square Mile Area, even though it is now
slated to become a 4.5 square-mile area. Many residents had suggested that the compromise plan was part of a government conspiracy to ease
them out of the neighborhood, but Pena said the new language suggests that the neighborhood is here to stay.

"It's a bit of a relief," she said. "We're very disappointed, though. We live in America. We're supposed to have rights."

The original Mod Waters plan would have protected the entire neighborhood, but park officials warned that it would also drain 30,000 acres of
Everglades wetlands, defeating the purpose of the plan. The compromise, they say, will allow true restoration.

NAACP Head Mfume Didn't Retire, He Was Booted Out
by Armstrong Williams
Posted Dec 6, 2004
   

Dont believe the well scripted press conference where former President and Chief Executive Officer of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, Kweisi Mfume, announced his resignation. Mfume did not resign from the nations oldest and most prestigious civil rights organization. He was kicked out, following a long simmering feud with NAACP Chairman Julian Bond. 

The two began feuding after Mfume nominated National Security Advisor Condoleezza Rice for his 2003 NAACP Image Award. Furious that Mfume was reaching out to the Bush administration, Bond responded by nominating "Boondocks" cartoonist Aaron McGruder for his Image Award. McGruder had ridiculed Rice in his comic strip and later called her a murderer for her role in the war in Iraq. 

The rift grew as Mfume continued to reach out to the Republican Party. Mfume realized that by reflexively voting Democrat in every election, the black voting populace has given away most of their political bartering power. After all, what incentive is there for either party to go out on a limb for blacks, if it is taken for granted that blacks will automatically vote Democrat? In effect, the black voting populace has created conditions that make it very easy for both parties to take them for granted. Mfume rightly reasoned that by reaching out to the Republican Party on issues that they already agree with -- like empowering faith based charities, supporting school vouchers, etc. -- the black voting populace can send the message that theyre no longer willing to blindly support the Democrats. Faced with the prospect of fleeing voters, the Democrats would be forced to make new overtures. This competition, in turn, would instill both parties with a sense of urgency for addressing those issues that black Americans routinely rate as their chief concerns. This competitive pressure would provide the black voting populace with increased political options -- and increased bartering power. Somehow this point was lost on Bond, who dug in his heels with mind numbing intransigence. Over the next year and a half, the rift became unmendable.

Ironically, it was Bond who handpicked Mfume to lead the organization in 1995. At the time, the NAACP was foundering amidst charges of sexual harassment and economic improprieties. We were four and a half million dollars in debt. We had scandal in the organization. Our very existence was threatened, recalls NAACP chairman, Julian Bond. Kweisi Mfume was the last person we interviewed, continued Bond. When he walked in the room, you could just see people thinking, weve got our man. 

Mfume promptly set about cutting the organizations employee base, raising money, and organizing overtly political coalitions. Within five years, the debt was gone and the NAACP was widely regarded as the most powerful political pressure group in the country. They alone had the ability to galvanize fifty million black votes. Members of the press found it all dazzling. Mfume not only has righted the ship, he also has set it on a new course, fawned USA Today columnist DeWayne Wickam. 

Bond and Mfume essentially partnered with the Democratic Party to revitalize the organization. Not surprisingly, the rhetoric coming out of the NAACP became increasingly partisan. During a speech before 2,000 attendees at the Ernest N. Morial Convention Center in New Orleans, NAACP Chairman Julian Bond proclaimed that President George W. Bush has "selected [political] nominees from the Taliban wing of American politics, appeased the wretched appetites of the extreme right wing and chosen cabinet officials whose devotion to confederacy is nearly canine in its uncritical affection." During a 2003 appearance at the National Press Club, Bond referred to the Republican Party as a crazed swarm of right wing locusts that have sought to subvert, ignore, defy and destroy the laws that require an America which is bias-free, Later that night Bond dubbed the Republicans, "the white people's party." 

Following the event, Mfume confronted Bond with his fear that the organization had become too outwardly political. Soon thereafter, the IRS launched investigation into whether Bonds remarks violated the organizations tax exempt status. 

The final tear came after the election. Mfume suggested sending a letter to President Bush, mapping out ways that they could work together to help the community. Bond rejected the idea. Mfume sent the letter anyway. To Bond, this was an unforgivable. A few weeks later, Bond had Mfume voted out. The message was clear: There is no room within the NAACP for intellectual diversity. Just loyal servitude to the Democratic Party. 

This is a crime. This is a shame. This is the sad state of the nations most storied civil rights organization.

Jerry,

Voucher socialism 

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
--

For years, the Right has promoted educational vouchers as an alternative to 
public schools. This has always been a delusion. The schools that take 
vouchers become the province of government regulators, while the money for 
the vouchers is taken out of the hide of taxpayers already being looted for 
public schools. Vouchers increase, not reduce, government involvement in 
education. 
Take a gander at the recently implemented and much-heralded Florida voucher 
program. Kids with good or even passable academic records are not eligible. 
Only the worst students from the worst public schools are allowed to use the 
voucher. Some voucher proponents hope to see this program expanded to 
everyone, but that still would not address the real issue. 

Leave aside their discriminatory impact and cost, and consider only their 
effect on schools themselves. At best, vouchers are an expensive attempt to 
reinvent the public schools, a doomed effort. At worst they are an attempt to 
force private schools to operate exactly like the public schools. Considering 
all the red tape the private school subjects itself to, they are a giant step 
in the wrong direction. (You can read the 181-page Florida law here.) 

After the government gets through with them, these private schools might as 
well be public schools. They must:

file huge and ongoing financial reports to the state (no internal privacy); 

submit to all federal anti-discrimination laws (no single sex or faith-based 
schools); 

accept scholarship students "on an entirely random and religious-neutral 
basis without regard to the student's past academic history" (dumb bunnies 
and Wiccans must be given the red carpet); 

only "employ or contract with teachers who hold a baccalaureate or higher 
degree, or have at least 3 years of teaching experience in public or private 
schools" (loving Moms need not apply); 

"accept as full tuition and fees the amount provided by the state for each 
student" (read: price controls); 

"agree not to compel any student attending the private school on an 
opportunity scholarship to profess a specific ideological belief, to pray, or 
to worship" (read: no independent curriculum); 

grant the government veto power over disciplinary procedures, such that no 
vouchered student can be kicked out.
We are talking about mountains of paperwork here, and a sacrifice of all 
independence. It's understandable that only a few private schools in Florida 
have been willing to subject themselves to the regulators. Let's hope that 
those who refuse this control don't face financial constraints that will suck 
them into the voucher system. 

The solution to this problem is not to repeal the regulations. So long as 
public money is involved, the government will always run the show -- as 
artists have surely figured out by now. The public, in fact, is right to 
expect some accountability in the way tax dollars are spent. The solution is 
to draw a strict line of separation between school and state by never 
permitting their finances to mix. 

But don't vouchers save money? Actually, the opposite is true. The Florida 
voucher plan will increase spending over present levels by $1.2 billion. 
Moreover, any money that is saved on tuition is not returned to the taxpayers 
but dumped back into the public school system. Making matters worse, public 
schools declared bad enough to permit their students to attend welfarized 
private schools get increased government funding. All told, taxpayers are 
going to be pillaged. 

No wonder the Left is increasingly interested in vouchers. It's a 
big-government program that increases, not reduces, the role of government in 
education, and will turn any institution taking vouchers into a carbon copy 
of state schools themselves. For example, the notoriously liberal Urban 
League of Miami argues for the constitutionality of vouchers, even though 
under federalism, their constitutionality shouldn't be in question (as versus 
their wisdom). What the Urban League likes is the welfarist aspect of the 
program. It's food stamps for education. 

Writing in the July 1999 Atlantic Monthly, liberal commentator Matthew Miller 
chides the Left for not seeing the inherent advantages of vouchers. They 
increase education spending, give preferences to the poor, and subject 
private schools to public control. From the socialist perspective, he asks, 
what's the problem? Good question. 

The real mystery is why conservatives, libertarians, or religious activists 
would cheer the Florida or any other voucher plan. Perhaps they have begun to 
believe their own neoconservative rhetoric about educational inequality, the 
plight of the poor who can't afford fancy schools, and the unjust privileges 
given those who can afford good schools. Notice how it is the schools, rather 
than the little darlings in them, that are always at fault? 

As a thought experiment, Miller proposes a new federal $8 billion spending 
program, so bad students in six big cities can take their F's and sometimes 
criminal behavior to private school at our expense. Incredibly, in 
interviews, Miller got Republican candidate-in-perpetuity Lamar Alexander and 
libertarian lawyer Clint Bolick of DC's Institute for Justice to endorse the 
idea. Again, that's a wholly new $8 billion federal program, endorsed by a 
self-proclaimed conservative and libertarian! 

If American education is to have a future, it's not through more government 
spending, control, and centralization. It is through increased local and 
private spending and control. The ideal is zero government involvement. Why 
does any freedom lover have to be reminded of that? 

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
--

Llewellyn H. Rockwell, Jr. is president of the Ludwig von Mises Institute

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

GOVERNOR BUSHS CONTINUES HISTORIC COMMITMENT TO PROTECT FLORIDAS UNIQUE ENVIRONMENT 
--Celebrates Everglades restoration & continued funding for Floridas landscape--
 
STUART -- Governor Jeb Bush this evening announced new initiatives in his upcoming 2001/02 budget recommendations that will further protect Floridas unique natural resources and environment. The Governor discussed his proposals during the Everglades Coalition Conference being held in Stuart, Florida.  He was joined by Department of Environmental Protection Secretary David B. Struhs, who, along with Governor Bush, was a recipient of the "Year 2000 Steward of the Everglades" award, presented by the Coalition.  
 
The Governor credited the bipartisan cooperation by members of Congress including Rep. Clay Shaw, Sen. Bob Graham, Sen. Connie Mack, and former Florida state Rep. Lee Constantine, and Florida state Senator Burt Saunders for the historic commitment of state and federal funding to restore America's Everglades.  This plan marks the nation's largest restoration project in history.   
 
"My budget proposal this year reflects the continued commitment of this administration to take care of our states precious environment, including the restoration of the River of Grass, said Governor Bush. "We have a responsibility to protect the natural resources that make Floridas landscape truly unique and provide our citizens with the opportunity to enjoy living in a quality environment.
 
Among the Governors proposals is $800,000 for preliminary work involving the restoration of the Ocklawaha River; $2.5 million for preserving Florida's springs, $7 million for manatee protection, $100 million state commitment for Everglades restoration, an additional $750,000 for water quality improvements to the Everglades, and $300 million for the Florida Forever program.
 
Ocklawaha River restoration
 
Over the summer, Governor Bush announced his support for the restoration of the Ocklawaha River, which has been impeded for 30 years by the Rodman Dam, creating the 9,000-acre Rodman Reservoir. During this period, nutrients have been collected in this impoundment. The effect of these nutrients, such as nitrates, must be considered as part of the river restoration plan. It is believed that without addressing the nutrient problem, the lower St. John's River would be adversely impacted once the dam is breached.
 
 
 
(more)
Specifically, the $800,000 budget request for the Ocklawaha River restoration project is intended to address the nutrient issue by providing:
 
*        $600,000 to develop a mitigation plan that identifies corrective projects to reduce nitrogen loading, including project design and cost estimates. These projects are expected to include actions such as implementation of best management practices for current land uses that are contributing nitrogen to the system and construction of treatment marshes for nitrogen removal.  
*        $200,000 to begin the cleanup of Silver Springs..(Jamie DeLoach)
 
 
 
 
Preserving Florida's springs
 
Florida has a unique treasure in its freshwater springs. More than 600 springs -- 33 of which are first magnitude springs(clarify???)-- dot the state's landscape from central to north Florida. These provide a number of assets to the state, from habitat to recreational opportunities, to drinking water supply.  The Governor's budget request proposes $2.5 million for developing public-private partnerships to further protect these vital components of Florida's natural environment.
 
Realizing that good science supports good decision making, the DEP will conduct research that will allow cause-and-effect relationships to be established between land use and water management activities and resulting changes in spring water quality and quantity. Additionally, $1 million will be allocated to four water management districts with first magnitude springs to provide grants for spring water cleanup. Landowners, citizens and government working as a team can make a difference. Therefore, Spring Basin Working Groups will be formed and supported. These groups will engage citizens and agencies in the protection and restoration of spring water quality and quantity.
 
 
America's Everglades restoration 
 
The fiscal year 2001-02 Executive Budget provides a second-year $100 million allocation for the "Save Our Everglades" Trust fund for the restoration project -- a total state cash commitment to date of $205 million. The Executive Budget also includes $750,000 to continue Advanced Treatment Technology research and monitoring to evaluate the cost effectiveness of various types of biological treatment systems to be incorporated into stormwater treatment areas already under construction in South Florida.
 
Under the funding plan approved by the Legislature in 2000, this year's installment will allow the state to build a recurrent source of funding. Through this approach, Florida will be able to meet funding needs that will peak in the near future before declining in later years of the restoration effort.
 
(more)
Manatee protection
 
Florida has some of the most endangered large terrestrial and marine mammals in the world. Based on an aerial survey, it is estimated that only 2,200 Florida manatees remain. Due to the growing number of manatee deaths in Florida waters, Governor Bush initiated a comprehensive protection plan that included last year's "Manatee Summit." The summit brought together interested parties from throughout the state to develop mutually agreeable solutions to reduce the boating-related mortality of manatees while balancing the interests of thousands of boaters who use Florida's waters.
 
The Executive Budget includes $7 million for Florida manatee protection efforts.  These include information and education campaigns, boat access facility planning and permitting, development of manatee protection plans, enhanced sanctuaries and refuges, and increased enforcement of slow speed and no wake zones. An additional $2 million will provide funding for increased overtime pay for marine patrol officers who enforce boating laws and manatee protections zones. The Governor is also proposing an increase of $50 in the fines for vessel speeding violations to support improved protection of the manatee. Additional funds of $350,000 are recommended for an "automatic planting" pilot project to restore sea grasses in estuaries and $63.8 million for law enforcement activities to protect the public and our biological resources.
 
 
The Florida Forever Program
 
Florida Forever -- a $3-billion, 10-year land and water protection and management program is the largest conservation program in the nation. Over the last 10 years, Florida has acquired 1.4 million acres of land and water areas throughout the state at an estimated expenditure of $2.4 billion. These lands and waters represent the best examples of Florida's remaining natural areas.
 
The Governor is recommending $300 million for the acquisition and protection of conservation and recreation land resources.  Projects will include ensuring there is a sufficient quantity of fresh water to meet current and future needs and increasing and preserving public recreation opportunities, archaeological and historic sites, forest lands, and green space and parks in urban areas.

Parents' Day, 2006 
A Proclamation by the President of the United States of America 
As a child's first teachers, mentors, and role models, parents shape the character of those who will help to build the future of our Nation. On Parents' Day, we pay tribute to the hard work and sacrifice of the millions of devoted parents who provide guidance, support, and unconditional love to their children. 
Mothers and fathers help kindle imaginations, inspire a love of learning, nurture the formation of young minds, and give children the courage and the drive to realize their dreams. By instilling in children the difference between right and wrong, parents guide their children toward developing into successful adults and responsible citizens who lead lives of purpose. In addition, the commitment of parents to the welfare of young people strengthens families and communities throughout our great country. 
My Administration supports grants and programs to promote healthy marriages and responsible fatherhood. The No Child Left Behind Act is helping us ensure that every child has the opportunity to learn, and recognizes that parental involvement is a vital part of the success of schools across America. Federal, State, and local programs, and faith-based and community groups provide additional resources to help parents as they work to raise children of conviction and character. 
On this special day, we express our deep gratitude to parents for their dedication to a bright and hopeful future for their children. We also pray for parents in the military who stand up for America, and we resolve that their sacrifice will always be honored by a grateful Nation. 
NOW, THEREFORE, I, GEORGE W. BUSH, President of the United States of America, by virtue of the authority vested in me by the Constitution and laws of the United States and consistent with Public Law 103-362, as amended, do hereby proclaim Sunday, July 23, 2006, as Parents' Day. I call upon citizens, private organizations, and governmental bodies at all levels to engage in activities and educational efforts that recognize, support, and honor parents, and I encourage American sons and daughters to convey their love, respect, and appreciation to their parents. 
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this twelfth day of July, in the year of our Lord two thousand six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and thirty-first. 
GEORGE W. BUSH

Dear Kayseas Grandmother:

 

Thank you for taking the time to write to Governor Bush regarding the Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test (FCAT). The Governor has forwarded your email to me  for response.

  

I know how frustrated you must be.  However, research shows that social promotion (promotion from one grade to the next based on a students age or other factors) is more harmful to a child in the long run than retention of the child in the early school years.   Children  who cannot read with comprehension at least by the fourth grade will perform poorly in every single area of instruction for the rest of their educational career.  The social promotion law requires that students who are not reading at grade level in the third grade, as demonstrated by scoring a Level one, the lowest level, on the reading portion of the FCAT, must be retained.  However, the law provides that a school board may exempt the following students from mandatory retention:

 

·            Limited English proficient students who have had less than two years of instruction in an English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) program;

·            Students with disabilities whose individual education plan indicates that participation in the FCAT is not appropriate;  

·            Students who demonstrate an acceptable level of performance on an alternative standardized reading assessment approved by the State Board of Education;

·            Students who demonstrate, through a student portfolio, that they are reading on grade level;  

·            Students with disabilities who participate in the FCAT and who have received intensive remediation in reading for more than two years but still demonstrate a deficiency in reading and were previously retained in kindergarten, first grade, second grade, or third grade; 

·            Students who have received intensive remediation in reading for two or more years but still demonstrate a deficiency in reading and who were previously retained in kindergarten, first grade, second grade, or third grade for a total of two years.  

 

As you can see by the above exemptions to mandatory retention, poor performance on the reading portion of the FCAT does not automatically mean that a third grade student will be retained.   Additionally, the social promotion law does not require students that are not in the third grade to be retained if they score a level one on the reading portion of the FCAT.  The decision to promote or retain these students rests solely with the local school district.  

 

Students in kindergarten through third grade are taught how to read. However, in grades four through the rest of their education students must be able to read in order to learn.  This is the reason it is so critical for students to become proficient readers before they leave third grade. Struggling readers who have been retained in the third grade are given a second chance to become proficient readers.  

 

You also requested contact information for someone in Lee County who could provide you with more information regarding this policy.  For more information regarding the third grade retention policy in Lee County please contact Dr. Constance Jones, Chief Academic Officer by calling (239) 337-8308.

 

I hope this  information  proves helpful to you.  Thank you again for taking the time to write to Governor Bush.

 

Sincerely,

 

 

J. Marleen Ahearn

Education Policy Coordinator

Death Row Inmate Dies of Cancer 
The Associated Press

RAIFORD, Fla. (AP) - A death row inmate died of natural causes at the Union Correctional Institution, the state Department of Corrections said Sunday. 

Robert Teffeteller, who was sentenced to death in 1985 for a murder in Volusia County six years earlier, died late Saturday night in the prison's infirmary. 

Teffeteller, 46, had been suffering from cancer, according to Department of Corrections spokesman C.J. Drake. 

"It was something that we were monitoring," Drake said. 

Teffeteller is the seventh death row inmate to die of natural causes since the beginning of 1999. There are 369 inmates remaining on Florida's death row.

Doctors may be key to reform

With some patients wary, Gov. Bush is trying to win doctors' support for his plan 

By ALISA ULFERTS, Times Staff Writer
Published January 16, 2005

  _____  

to turn much of Medicaid over to private insurers. 

TALLAHASSEE - Dr. David McKalip says he knows insurance companies don't have the best reputation for quickly approving treatments.

But dealing with private health plans is a walk in the park compared to Medicaid, the St. Petersburg brain and spine surgeon said last week.

"The state does not provide a lot of the services I want for my patients," said McKalip. Medicaid, the state-federal health care program for the poor, often approves surgery instead of noninvasive pain management treatments McKalip would prefer.

And the state often is less flexible about different treatment paths.

So McKalip said he was happy to hear Gov. Jeb Bush has proposed turning over much of the Medicaid system to insurance companies.

"If you take the decisionmaking out of the hands of government and put it in the hands of doctors and patients, you're going to get a better outcome," McKalip said.

Bush is counting on more doctors like McKalip as he attempts to revamp Medicaid, whose runaway costs are expected to reach $17-billion next year.

But the plan is so vague at this point that few people are willing to say whether they like it or not.

"They probably don't know yet," said Alan Levine, secretary of Florida's Agency for Health Care Administration. "I'm going to meet with them and talk to them about it."

Luring more doctors 

The evolution of Bush's proposal is being watched closely by Medicaid patients and their doctors, who may find themselves on opposing sides once the details are released. Bush has said he hopes to have the plan approved by federal regulators and state lawmakers by the end of the year.

Patients have voiced concern that reining in costs means fewer benefits. Doctors say they hope Bush replaces government bureaucrats with physicians who will decide what gets covered, and that he raises reimbursement rates, which have been stagnant the past few years.

Bush has said he hopes the changes will persuade more doctors to take Medicaid patients, who have a hard time finding doctors in some parts of the state, such as the Panhandle.

Dr. Marcy Solomon Baker, for example, devotes about 10 percent of her Tampa pediatric practice to Medicaid patients. She said that's the maximum she can afford to maintain. The cumbersome regulations, paired with anemic reimbursements, caused Baker to reject new Medicaid patients. She said she knows other pediatricians who have dropped Medicaid patients altogether.

State officials say the scarcity of physicians makes the program inefficient and contributes to higher costs. Fewer doctors means less coordination of patients' care, which can lead to expensive duplication of tests and services and delays in treatment that can result in costly and unhealthy complications.

By paying HMOs and other health companies to care for Medicaid patients, the state hopes to get ready-made networks of physicians and specialists more experienced than the state at effectively and efficiently treating patients. Unlike the state, most private health plans also have programs to encourage healthy living, like smoking cessation, weight loss and disease management classes that can reduce their need for costly treatments.

Enticing insurers 

To entice insurance companies and other managed care entities to take on some of Florida's sickest, poorest residents, Bush has suggested a cap on Medicaid benefits, just as private insurance plans have. That would ease some of the financial risk for insurance companies.

Patients requiring more care would be covered by a catastrophic fund financed through a percentage of Medicaid premiums.

Baker said she hopes this will make it easier for her and other doctors to treat Medicaid patients.

"On the surface, it actually sounds good," Baker said of Bush's plan.

Annie Henderson said she is less sure.

The 55-year-old former corrections officer from Marianna can't walk from her bedroom to her kitchen without tugging at the long tube that feeds her diseased lungs the pure oxygen they need to function. She has been in the hospital twice in the past two months for pneumonia.

Medicaid paid the bill for each of those hospital visits, plus the $1,000 she spends every month on drugs and equipment.

Henderson doesn't disagree that Medicaid could be streamlined to work better for her and for physicians. But her biggest concern is that very sick patients like her could get lost in the managed care maze.

"It might cover my basics, but if I get pneumonia, will it cover that?" Henderson said. "If if changes so much that is doesn't cover as much, that could be life threatening." Bush's proposal calls for managed care companies and other networks to design the plans Medicaid patients would use.

Basic services, such as doctors' visits, prescription drugs, diagnostic tests and emergency services covered by the state's mandatory and optional Medicaid programs would be covered. Beyond that, it would be up to the managed care networks to attract patients by offering additional services or conveniences, such as better prescription coverage or a network that includes pediatric specialists.

Milton Reed says he doesn't buy it.

"Right now, I get to see any doctor I want," said Reed, a 67-year-old Palm Coast resident and Medicaid beneficiary who suffers from heart trouble, asthma, emphysema and high blood pressure.

"My mama always said, if it ain't broke, don't fix it," Reed said.

HOW MEDICAID WORKS: 

A prospective patient fills out an application, which is processed by the state Department of Children and Families. Generally, Medicaid serves pregnant women, children, the frail elderly and the disabled who earn as much as 150 percent of the federal poverty level, or just more than $18,000 for a family of four.

If approved for Medicaid, most patients choose a primary physician from a list of those who accept Medicaid. That doctor is paid $3 a month to coordinate a patient's care, such as controlling access to specialists. Doctors bill Medicaid directly for treatments.

Nearly a third of Medicaid patients already are enrolled in an HMO, which receives a premium from the state to cover their care.

HOW BUSH'S PLAN WOULD WORK:

All 2.3-million Medicaid patients would enroll in an HMO or other managed care network. The state would calculate a premium for each patient based on individual health risks. The network of the patient's choice would be paid a premium to provide care. The state would provide counselors to help Medicaid patients choose a health plan.

To reduce risk to insurance companies, the state would cap Medicaid benefits at a certain level. Patients needing more care would be covered by a catastrophic fund.

From:	hardingbill@bellsouth.net
Sent:	Sunday, June 27, 2004 7:21 PM
To:	Jeb Bush
Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Bill Harding 2405 Bayshore Dr Belleair Beach, Fl 33786 United States

Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

MONICA BOONE 2016 CROSBY AVENUE PITTSBURGH, PA 15216 United States

Betties----pls print for Gov and Kathleen.  Betty H.---does Gov have a call and work time available?
Governor----Congressman Weldons COS called today.  Dr. Weldon met with Sec ONeil re the Florida Non-Resident Alien banking regulation that Florida Bankers have been very worried about and that we have worked for about 1 year.  Below is a brief description of the issue and a short timeline.
Dr. Weldon would like to speak with you this week, about his conversation with Sec ONeil and hopes that you can light more fire in the Administration to get them to pull the proposed regulation.  Our office has had several contacts with the FL Bankers about this issue and with Treasury and the WH.  I get the sense that the Congressman would like this to be our number one issue.
Background.
Florida's bankers are concerned about an IRS-proposed regulation that would require banks to report all interest of $10 or more earned by non-resident aliens on their depositswhich the US government would then share with the aliens' home countries.  The U.S. government sees this as a way to better track possible terrorist assets while encouraging communication and coordination among nations fighting money laundering.
However, according to the Florida Bankers Association (FBA),  this regulation would force wealthy individuals to withdraw their funds from US banks and seek financial shelter elsewhere due to a fear of kidnapping or terrorism in their home countries if the scope of their wealth were disclosed.  Currently, Florida holds approximately $49 billion in foreign assets, the majority of which originates in Latin America.  If the IRS began implementation of the regulation, the FBA estimates that Florida would lose $18-$34 billion and 62,000-188,000 jobs in the first year alone.
Timeline.
-          By May 7, 01, Frank Bonner had talked to IRS, I spoke with Asst Sec at Treasury and Kathleen spoke with ONeils Chief of Staff.
-          May 17, 01, Frank Bonner attended a meeting with FBA and Senate Committee Staff (we set the meeting).
-         May 17, 01, Frank Bonner attended meetings with FBA and Treasury and WH staff.
-         The Governor wrote a letter on June 7, 2001 to Secretary O'Neill asking for a careful review of the regulation and for Treasury to look for a better solution to the problem of money-laundering/collaboration.
-         October 1, 01, the FBA and Florida International Bankers Association sent a letter to Secretary O'Neill including an impact study they had commissioned to look into the damages of this regulation (Tony Villamil completed the study).
-         October 17, 01, representatives of FBA, came to Washington to meet with Pippa Malmgren and Marc Weinburger (Dept. of Treasury) to discuss the issue, and inform the Department about the implications of the regulation.  The same day, the group also met with Congressman Weldon, Congressman Davis and staff from Senator Graham's office.

Dear Sir:  do not allow the  Agri People to continue their pollution of the Everglades. Make DEP hold them to the lowest standard possible! --------------------
Sugar growers, farmers want to pour more pollution into Everglades 
--------------------

By Neil Santaniello
Staff Writer

August 22, 2001

In a battle forming over the amount of phosphorus that will be allowed in the Everglades, the sugar industry is expected to push for permission to pour perhaps twice as much of the pollutant into the `Glades as scientists say is found in its pristine areas.

Phosphorus is found in unspoiled parts of the Everglades at levels below or around 10 parts per billion, say scientists from the South Florida Water Management District.

At a public meeting Thursday before state regulators, the sugar industry and other farmers are expected to argue that they should be allowed to pour 15 to 20 parts per billion, or more. Their numbers are based on findings from their own studies.

"It may sound like a very mundane and boring technical dialogue but a lot is at stake here," said Ernie Barnett, director of ecosystem projects for the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. "Both sides are pretty polarized."

According to an Audubon of Florida official, if the limit goes higher than 10 parts per billion, "the Everglades dies."

The scientific analysis out there "all seems to irrevocably point to 10 parts per billion as the appropriate criterion," Charles Lee, the group's senior vice president, said.

Farmers -- whose sugar and vegetable fields south of Lake Okeechobee are producing most of the phosphorus pollution entering the Everglades -- could face higher cleanup bills for the ecosystem if their suggested standard doesn't prevail. Growers are paying a portion of a $800 million Everglades cleanup bill also shouldered by taxpayers.

When phosphorus pours into the Everglades at levels higher than 10 parts per billion, it alters the marsh landscape, replacing signature knife-edged sawgrass with dense stands of cattails. The fertilizer is washed into the marsh along with agricultural storm water.

By holding phosphorus to 10 parts per billion, "you are really getting down to [the amount found in] rainwater," Barnett said. "You're really getting pretty pure."

Debate on the matter should grow hotter starting on Thursday at a public meeting in West Palm Beach before Florida's Environmental Regulation Commission and the DEP.

Water managers have been building more than 47,000 acres of filter marshes on the northern lip of the Everglades to sift phosphorus from the dirty farm water. But their stormwater treatment areas only reduce the wetland pollutant to about 22 parts per billion.

The pollution standard at issue will determine how much more the water must be cleaned.

Barbara Miedema, spokeswoman for the Sugar Cane Growers Cooperative, said the marsh may be better off with a range of allowable amounts of phosphorus, since it is home to sawgrass plains and other types of wilderness-like tree islands.

The Environmental Regulation Commission -- a seven-member environmental rule-making body -- will take up the subject at 9 a.m. at the DEP's Southeast District Office, 400 N. Congress Ave. Other public meetings will follow.

Under a 1994 state law called the Everglades Forever act, the regulation commission has a deadline of December 2003 to adopt an official standard, which won't be enforced for three years after that.

The DEP, which has been studying the issue, will make a recommendation to the regulation commission, which can then reject, accept or modify it.

In a strange twist for environmental advocacy, Audubon of Florida and environmental groups say they would prefer that the regulation commission set no pollution limit at all.

Their reason: If the regulators fail to propose a standard, 10 or otherwise, state law provides a default. That figure is 10.

But if the regulation commission adopts a number, that standard can be challenged before a state administrative law judge, who does not have to give a greater weight to the findings of environmental regulators than to special interests. Environmentals fear that situation.

"We think that would be a travesty for government agencies ... to fail to act," said Miedema, with the sugar cane cooperative. "It's not using taxpayer dollars wisely."

Florida already has a phosphorus limit for the Everglades but it takes the form of a "narrative," not numeric, standard. It says basically that phosphorus entering the marsh cannot cause "an imbalance of natural populations of aquatic flora and fauna."

The phrasing is harder to enforce than a numeral.

The DEP has not yet chosen a standard to push, but it likely will be in the low end of the 10 to 20 range, Barnett said.

To:	Jeb Bush
Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Rob Dolton 27 Burns Close Horsham, W Sussex Rh12 5PF United Kingdom

Is Your Property In Danger? 

 

I want to alert you to a landmark legal decision (Wayne County v. Hathcock)* that could affect your property or the property of your neighbors, family, or friends.  It is a new decision that will have nationwide implications. For property owners, who own prime real estate, it might be the only thing that balances the unalienable right to own your property with the governments despotic power of eminent domain to take from one citizen and give to another. Please share this information with other property owners in Jupiter and elsewhere.

 

For the last 20 years, if private property could be put to a better use i.e. its a public benefit to have a condo or business on that street instead of your house or business; or if it would generally benefit the public by improving the Towns business image; or if it would create jobs and tax dollars, then the Town could claim it through Eminent Domain. Courts looked the other way to the abuses.

 

In fact, if there were economic benefit, it validated practically any excuse to take a citizens property.  Ownership of private property was forever subject to the governments determination that another private party would put it to a better use.  Ownership of real property was always in jeopardy and it was quite common for government condemnation to benefit private profit. 

 

The usual victims of eminent domain abuses are citizens who are not politically influential. A citizen is confronted by the full legal power of the local and state governments, who assert a practically boundless authority to take the persons property against his will.  Exposed to extreme psychological and political pressure, he will generally acquiesce in the condemnation because he rarely can afford good legal representation to bring a serious challenge.

 

The result is that citizens are subject to the most outrageous confiscation of their property for the benefit of private investors. This perpetuates an unfair form of corporate welfare by which unconsenting private citizens are forced to subsidize the profits of the politically favoreda classic David-and-Goliath. 

 

On August 4, 2004, the Michigan Supreme Court corrected its 20-year failed Redevelopment Experiment by outlawing abuse of eminent domain power. This decision should dissuade our local government from trying it in the Inlet Village along A1A; however, the Town has already shown their despotic power by trying to take 2.5 miles of private waterfront property located on the Intracoastal and Inlet simply by passing Regulations that give it to the Town.

 

Watch the scenario carefully as it unfolds. Florida courts have not yet looked at any appeals in light of this Michigan eminent domain decision.  If the Town of Jupiter tries to further grab private property in the Redevelopment District called the Inlet Village by condemning and transferring the properties to a developer, it will surely provide the Florida Courts an opportunity to concur with this new limitation unfolded in the landmark Michigan case. 

*  http://courts.michigan.gov/supremecourt/Clerk/Opinions-03-04-Term/124070.pdf

AP - Senate passes condemnation limits, refuses exceptions 
 
BILL KACZOR 
 
Associated Press Writer 
 
 
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (AP) _ Legislation limiting the ability of local
governments to condemn homes and other property for private
redevelopment cleared the Florida Senate on Thursday after the chamber
refused to make an exception for a massive renewal project in Riviera
Beach. 

The Senate passed a proposed state constitutional amendment (HJR 1569)
38-2 and a bill (HB 1567) 37-3. Both measures returned to the House,
which previously had approved them, because the Senate made some
modifications. 

Rep. Marco Rubio, R-Miami, filed both measures in response to a U.S.
Supreme Court decision that last year upheld condemnation for economic
development in a Connecticut case. 

That unleashed a firestorm of outrage across the nation. Florida is
among 47 states that have passed or are considering measures to limit or
ban condemning property and turning it over to developers. 

``There is probably nothing hotter in the minds of the folks (back home)
than the Supreme Court decision on eminent domain,'' said Sen. Jim King,
R-Jacksonville. ``They accept the fact that property rights is a
God-given, by our forefathers, right.'' 

The bill would go into effect immediately upon becoming law and put a
halt to projects already under way or in the planning stages. The
amendment would take effect Jan. 2 if approved by voters. 

A proposal to also put a delayed effective date in the bill failed on a
voice vote. It was offered by Sen. Mandy Dawson, D-Fort Lauderdale. She
argued it would be unfair to Riviera Beach to force the city to give up
a $2.4 billion plan to redevelop blighted areas into upscale
condominiums and shops and a marina after years of work on it. 

Riviera Beach Mayor Michael Brown said the city is prepared to challenge
the bill in court, if it becomes law. 

``I think we can make a strong argument that we are entitled to follow
the old rules,'' Brown said. ``Communities like ours always seem to get
the short end of the stick.'' 

Riviera Beach is a pocket of poverty with a largely minority population
in otherwise affluent Palm Beach County. Brown said the
condemnation-limiting measures would help destroy cities such as his. 

Hurricane ``Katrina did that to New Orleans and the Legislature is doing
that in Florida,'' Brown said. 

Riviera Beach's situation received little sympathy in Tallahassee. 

Sen. Nancy Argenziano, R-Crystal River, argued that if private
developers want land for their projects they should pay owners what they
want to sell instead of getting it at a bargain-basement price through
condemnation. 

``This bill only deals with the transfer of property ... taking property
from one person and transferring ownership to someone else,'' said Sen.
Daniel Webster, R-Winter Haven, the Senate sponsor. 

Webster stressed that it would not affect the ability of local
governments to condemn property for roads, utilities and other
traditional public uses. 

Dawson and two other Democrats, Gary Siplin of Orlando and Frederica
Wilson of Miami, voted against the bill. 

Sen. Les Miller, D-Tampa, and Argenziano voted against the amendment.
Argenziano said she was sticking to her policy of opposing changes in
the Florida Constitution although she is a strong supporter of property
rights.

The word "inalienable" means that the rights in question cannot be given away or transferred to another by law. Now, by allowing Michael Schiavo to starve his wife to death, Judge George W. Greer transfers to Schiavo the exercise of her right to life, doing on her behalf what the Florida state constitution declares she herself could not do (since an inalienable right cannot be given away). 

Schiavo's decision, and any element of the law it is based on that has the same effect, are therefore unconstitutional on the face of it.

HEALTH
Dems Urge Administration To Reverse Medicaid Decision
Several leading Democrats are urging the Bush administration to reconsider what appears to be a policy to reverse a law designed to ensure that Medicaid recipients have reasonable access to emergency room care. House Energy and Commerce ranking member John Dingell, D-Mich., along with other Democrats on his committee and Sen. Jeff Bingaman, D-N.M., sent a letter to HHS Secretary Thompson today, protesting the policy change. "In this instance it is not simply a matter of inaction to correct a wrong, but rather an affirmative action to weaken existing protections," they wrote.
As first reported in CongressDaily Thursday, a Dec. 20 letter from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to state Medicaid administrators appears to instruct states that they can restrict Medicaid recipients access to emergency room care. The Democrats contend that instruction violates a 1997 healthcare law that would allow Medicaid recipients to receive covered care at the nearest emergency room if they reasonably believe they are experiencing an emergency. Dingell said the consequences of the policy change would burden hospitals, which are seeking additional federal payments to help stay afloat.
Meanwhile, Senate Majority Leader Frist Thursday told Tennessee reporters that Congress will have to do something to help states deal with growing Medicaid expenditures at a time when most states are struggling with budget deficits, although he did not offer specifics. "At the end of the day we've got to address it because Medicaid is a state-administered program, but it is principally funded by the federal government," he said, according to the Memphis Commercial-Appeal. Tennessee is one of the states struggling with budget problems, and Frist played a significant role in designing a restructuring of that state's Medicaid program, now called TennCare, when he was a physician in private practice.  by April Fulton

From:	wierzi@dog-cards.de
Sent:	Tuesday, June 29, 2004 2:12 PM
To:	Jeb Bush
Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Ralf Wierz Duisburger Str.10 Berlin, Berlin 10707 Germany
