Eminent domain legislation in response to the United States Supreme Court decision in   Kelo v. New London is being considered in 42 of the 43 states that have gone into session so far this year.  Bills have been enacted in 12 states-Alabama, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Kentucky, Maine, Nebraska, South Dakota, Utah, Vermont, West Virginia and Wisconsin.  Pennsylvania has passed legislation that is awaiting the governor's action.  New Hampshire passed a constitutional amendment that will go on the ballot in November for voter approval.  The governor vetoed legislation that passed the legislature in New Mexico.  

In reading the bills from the 12 states, it appears that we are clearly at the top as far as strength of our legislation. We are the only state so far to have a Ballot initiative and a statutory fix. The only missing element from a stronger comparison I have found is that Indiana requires a payment of 150% of fair market value for a condemned residence.  Our bill does not require a specific amount for compensation. 

The legislation generally falls into seven categories:

*	Prohibiting eminent domain for economic development purposes, to generate tax revenue, or to transfer private property to another private entity. 

*	Defining what constitutes "public use," generally the possession, occupation or enjoyment of the property by the public at large, public agencies or public utilities. 

*	Restricting eminent domain to blighted properties and redefining what constitutes blight to emphasize detriment to public health or safety. 

*	Requiring greater public notice, more public hearings, negotiation in good faith with landowners and approval by elected governing bodies. 

*	Requiring compensation greater than fair market value where property condemned is the principal residence. 

*	Placing a moratorium on eminent domain for economic development. 

*	Establishing legislative study committees or stakeholder task forces to study and report back to legislature with findings.

 
Will provide you more information as it becomes available. 

Janice

School Excels in Reading by Sticking With What Works
         
By RICHARD LEE COLVIN, Times Staff Writer

WASHINGTON -- From outside, Seaton Elementary School doesn't look like a
national model for anything, except maybe urban decay. The windows of the
beige brick building are barred, the garden out back is littered with beer
bottles, and the adjacent blocks are scarred by the crumbling hulks of
once-graceful brownstones.

But after being buzzed in past the security doors, a visitor can see reading
taught with an intensity and structure that the Bush administration wants to
replicate across the country.

Test scores have soared at Seaton, as has enthusiasm for reading. That has
happened despite characteristics that have been barriers to learning
elsewhere: Virtually all of Seaton's students are poor enough to qualify for
federally subsidized meals, and English is not the first language for a
third of them.

"These kids can do it . . . regardless of what people think, as long as
they're given appropriate instruction," said Seaton Principal Willy Lamb.
"Not that they don't come with some issues. But what we're trying to do is
deal with those issues while still teaching them."

The school is being used to bolster the argument that the nation's schools
should stop embracing instructional fads and begin teaching lessons grounded
in cognitive and educational science.

That culture shift is laid out in the education reform bill signed by
President Bush in January. The Education Department will hand out more than
$5 billion over the next five years for states to promote teaching reading
based on what the legislation calls "scientifically based reading research."

Not philosophy. Not instinct. Not hope. Science.

At Seaton recently, preschoolers clamored over an inflated plastic doll
called "Miss F" and begged for the chance to write the letter on the
chalkboard. Then they all stood and stretched, touching their "fingers" to
their "feet."

Such a lesson is based on research that has found that even 3-year-olds
enjoy learning letters and sounds, giving them an early and fun start on
skills crucial for actual reading.

Here, children begin reading in kindergarten. In one class, the children
gathered around teacher Mary Hale could barely contain themselves as they
repeated phrases such as "Andy Apple is an acrobat" and read in unison words
rhyming with "at."

Second-graders during a recent visit were writing a response to a story
using words such as "quarrel" and "warrior." And in a fifth-grade class,
every student was able to flawlessly and passionately read his or her lines
in a play about the Underground Railroad heroics of Harriet Tubman.

None of that was happening five years ago. That's when Seaton became one of
nine District of Columbia schools in a federally sponsored study of the
effects of a structured phonics program bolstered by intensive teacher
training.

The difference, said veteran fourth-grade teacher Mary Woods, is "almost
like night and day. These kids have a cockiness and a self-confidence
because they know how to attack words."

That pleases Susan B. Neuman, assistant U.S. secretary of Education in
charge of overseeing the overhaul of reading lessons nationally.

She began her career three decades ago in Berkeley, teaching in an open
classroom of first-, second- and third-graders. Back then, she said, the
dominant progressive philosophy held that children's natural curiosity would
help them learn to read more or less on their own. Neuman and colleagues
didn't so much as teach, she said, as they "trailed the children as they
went through activity, activity, activity."

Some children did learn to read. But many did not. And they suffered the
consequences, Neuman recently told educators gathered in Washington from 23
states to learn about the administration's Reading First and Early Reading
First programs.

She left teaching after eight years for what was to turn out to be an
illustrious career as a reading researcher. But she used the experience of
seeing her students struggle as she sampled different techniques.

"We do have evidence. We do know what works," Neuman told the educators.

The evidence was summed up in 2000 by the National Reading Panel, mandated
by Congress. To tap into the new federal reading money, states will have to
agree to promote teaching consistent with its findings.

The money is far more than has ever before been made available. California
alone stands to receive $134 million from the program this year and $147
million next year.

Typically, the federal government has left such decisions to the states.
And, reading policy varies greatly. California, for example, already
mandates phonics in early reading lessons. Other states, such as
Connecticut, leave such decisions up to local districts.

In addition, for at least 50 years, the dogma of how best to teach reading
has swung from one extreme to another, often amid rancorous debate.

Recently, "whole language" approaches that encouraged children to intuit the
nuts and bolts of how words worked have been losing out to the direct
teaching of the sounds associated with letters.

Neuman said the administration's approach cannot properly be labeled either
"whole language" or "phonics." Rather, she said, it is comprehensive and
stresses direct teaching, as opposed to the student-centered activities
common when she began her career.

To read well, children need to know phonics and how letter sounds combine to
form words, the reading panel concluded. But they also need lessons focused
on vocabulary, reading fluently, writing and techniques to boost their
understanding.

Neuman and other administration officials point out that neither phonics nor
whole language alone has improved reading results. In fact, reading
achievement has stayed pretty much the same for decades.

The most recent national snapshot shows that 68% of the nation's
fourth-graders, for example, are not proficient readers, meaning they cannot
analyze challenging materials. Among children from low-income families, that
figure soars to 86%.

Though some say the standard is unrealistically high, the Bush
administration wants all children to be proficient readers within 12 years.

But some experts say the practices the administration promotes go well
beyond what the reading panel recommends.

P. David Pearson, dean of the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Education, said
the research cited by the panel says phonics lessons are effective in
kindergarten and first grade. Beyond that, he said, there's little evidence
to support their use.

Pearson said he also worries that the administration is putting too much
emphasis on what's known as phonemic awareness, or the skill of being able
to detect the individual sounds within words. The panel's research suggests
about 18 hours of such lessons are all that's necessary, he said. But widely
used commercial programs devote far more time than that to such training.

Donna Ogle, an Illinois professor who is president of the influential
International Reading Assn., praised the administration for spotlighting
reading. But she said better teaching by itself is not enough.

Where test scores are the lowest, she said, students move frequently, they
come to school hungry, discipline is lacking, class sizes are large and
buildings are often in disrepair.

"What we're doing to teachers and principals in the worst schools is
ignoring the context in which they're educating kids," Ogle said.

But the plan also has supporters, including major education groups
representing urban schools, school boards and teacher unions.

President Bush announced this month that the American Federation of Teachers
volunteered to work with the administration to spread the word.

The Los Angeles Unified School District, which began emphasizing phonics
from kindergarten to the second grade in 1999, is being cited as a success
story.

Ronnie Ephraim, administrator in charge of the L.A. Unified reading program,
told the group in Washington that most schools now spend more than three
hours daily on reading-related lessons. The district has invested millions
in training primary teachers, and students' progress is monitored every six
weeks, he said.

Reading scores for first-graders are now above the national average, up 21
points in two years; second-graders' scores are up by 50%; third-graders' by
30%. Such progress is winning over critics.

Anna Maria Martinez, principal of Murchison Elementary School in East Los
Angeles, said first-graders are talking about metaphors and writing "at
levels we had never seen before."

"For us, it was phenomenal," she said. She said veteran teachers, initially
skeptical, now are true believers and say "they'll never go back."

The district is using a phonics-based program called Open Court that is
gaining notice nationally. But Martinez said the investment in training
teachers has been as important to its success.

The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values. Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

The Case for 'Progressive' Vouchers 
Robert B.  <http://www.prospect.org/authors/reich-r.html> Reich

The Wall Street Journal 

Education tops the list of Americans' concerns. But there's no agreement on what to do about it. The biggest emerging battle is between people who advocate school choice and those who want more money for schools. George W. Bush wants to give vouchers to poor kids in failing schools so they, and their parents, can shop for a better education. 

But Al Gore says no way. He would prefer to spend $115 billion more on schools over the next 10 years, by contrast with the $13.5 billion over five years that Mr. Bush proposes . Joe Lieberman, who has sponsored legislation calling for experiments with vouchers for private schools, is now mute on the subject. Meanwhile, voucher plans in Cleveland and Florida are in the courts, and initiatives to authorize statewide voucher schemes will be on ballots this fall in California and Michigan. 

Vouchers Work 

The standoff between vouchers and money is predictable. It is also regrettable, because it prevents consideration of a most promising way to improve school performance-giving kids ''progressive vouchers that are inversely related to the size of their family's income. 

Evidence mounts that vouchers do work for kids who use them. A new study of students in New York, Washington and Dayton, Ohio--conducted by researchers at Harvard, Georgetown and the University of Wisconsin--found that after two years, the average performance of black students who switched to private schools was 6% higher than that of students who stayed behind in public schools. 

So why not simply "voucherize" all education funding and let students and their parents select where they can get the best education? After all, that's what wealthy and upper-middle-class families do by choosing pricey homes in upscale towns with excellent public schools (in which case the ''voucher" comes with the home), or by sending their kids to private schools. Voucher proponents, including a growing number of black parents, argue that poor kids should have the same advantage. 

The biggest drawback to vouchers is that kids who are most troublesome, or whose parents couldn't care less or are overwhelmed with other problems, would almost certainly end up bunched together in the worst schools. Such schools would become even worse than they were before. After all, the increasing concentration of poor kids in America's poor schools has already compounded the problems these kids and those schools must deal with. Assuming that the kids who leave these schools take public money with them, the worst schools would end up with fewer resources per difficult child. 

The new study also confirms the importance of school environment. The parents of voucher recipients noted the differences between their children's private schools and their former public schools, pointing out that there was less fighting, less destruction of property, and less racial conflict in the private schools than in the public schools their kids left behind. 

Why is behavior better in private schools? For one thing, private schools enforce discipline in ways that public schools cannot. In particular, private schools can expel a child who seriously misbehaves. About 20% of the students in the study who were selected to attend private schools never completed the two years. It seems a fair guess that at least some of them were sent packing. But public schools must, by law, provide a public education to all. The students drawn to private schools are also likely to be better behaved than those who remain in public schools. In the study I cite, most of the students already attending the private schools were from families who cared enough about their children to seek a good education for them, and who earned enough to afford one. By contrast, many inner-city public schools are comprised of students whose families are either unable to pay attention to their futures, or very poor, or both. 

There is a powerful case for giving every possible advantage to better-behaved poor kids who are fortunate enough to have caring parents. School vouchers offer them an escape route from troublesome and unmotivated peers, negative peer influences and anarchic environments where teachers have to spend much of their time trying to maintain order. But it also means that school vouchers alone won't solve the problem of poor kids and lousy schools. Vouchers may just concentrate the problem further. 

Almost a decade ago, New Zealand embarked on the closest thing we've seen to a national school-voucher experiment. Parents were given the right to choose the school their kids attended. This gave schools that attracted more applicants than they could accommodate great discretion over whom they accepted. The result: The best schools became even better, as they attracted the highest achievers. But the worst schools grew worse--with ever-greater concentrations of difficult-to-teach students from impoverished homes. Vouchers--with nothing more-- led to economic and social polarization. 

But polarization exists in the U.S. because of residential segregation by income as well as the stark relationship between a community's tax base and the quality of its schools. Poor kids are more likely to attend underfunded schools than kids who aren't poor. Analysis from the National Center for Education Statistics shows that most poor students live in districts that spend less per student than their state's average. The Department of Education recently reported that much of the teaching in America's poorest schools is being done by teacher's aides without college degrees, rather than by qualified teachers. 

The only way to begin to decouple poor kids from lousy schools is to give poor kids additional resources, along with vouchers enabling them and their parents to choose how to use them. Per-pupil public expenditures now average between $6,000 and $7,000 a year in the U.S. (with some states spending as much as $9,000, and others as little as $4,000. Ideally, a child from America's poorest 20% of families would receive a voucher worth between $10,000 and $12,000. Children from families in the next quintile would receive vouchers worth between $8,000 and $10,000. The vouchers could be used at any school that meets certain minimum standards, regardless of whether the school is now dubbed "public," "charter'' or ''private.'' (Leave aside, for now, the tricky First Amendment issue of public money for religious schools.) 

What would be the likely result of such progressive vouchers? Schools already in easy geographic reach of poor kids would get an immediate infusion of billions of dollars they could use to upgrade physical plants, buy new textbooks, initiate after-school programs, and hire more and better teachers. But they would also have to compete with other schools nearby which thought they could put those sizable vouchers to even better educational use. 

Even some suburban schools can be expected to enter the competition. The large vouchers would make it worthwhile to send vans to pick up and drop off groups of inner-city students. Although the most intensive competition would center on the best-behaved poor kids whose parents were most aggressive in seeking out good schools, the large vouchers would spur schools to recruit and retain more difficult children as well. Students, parents, and the schools they select would sign contracts for a minimum of two years, outlining their mutual objectives and responsibilities for meeting them. 

Wealthier suburban schools would have even greater incentive to compete for students from poor families if the progressive voucher extended all the way up the income ladder. If children from families in the top 20% of income got vouchers of, say, $2,000 to $4,000 a year, schools in wealthier communities would make every effort to seek out enough $l0,000 or $12,000 ''vouchered" students in their region to meet their budgets. 

The Challenge 

Do you like the idea? Don't hold your breath. A progressive voucher system is a very long shot for now. For it to become a reality, we would need a substantial overhaul of the financing of public education. This would entail pooling local property taxes from both rich and poor communities (which the rich are likely to resist with no less intensity than they've opposed state schemes to better equalize educational spending) and dramatically increasing federal and state funding. 

Teachers' unions may not look fondly upon the idea either, although it could result in higher salaries for good teachers. The largest challenge is to convince each side in the current education battle that they have only part of the answer, and their opponents have the other.

Governor----Congressman Weldons COS called today.  Dr. Weldon met with Sec ONeil re the Florida Non-Resident Alien banking regulation that Florida Bankers have been very worried about and that we have worked for about 1 year.  Below is a brief description of the issue and a short timeline.

If the IRS began implementation of the regulation, the FBA estimates that Florida would lose $18-$34 billion and 62,000-188,000 jobs in the first year alone.

Incentives and imagination key in effort to land Safire Aircraft

Ken Vandruff
When the prize is a 500,000-square-foot facility with the potential for 1,000 jobs, economic development teams from targeted regions work hard to put together the best possible incentive package. 

They also play their hands very close to the vest. They don't want competitors to know what they've offered. 

That's why Wichita economic development officials won't comment on what discussions they've had with Safire Aircraft Co. 

The start-up light business jet company is building a prototype at its Miami, Fla., facility with a goal of a first flight this year. But Gregory Fatovic, Safire's vice president and general counsel, says the company needs a final assembly plant ready for production in 2006. 

"Some of the potential investors that are looking at the company are the ones that suggested, 'Look at Wichita because that's the capital of general aviation,' " he says. 

Fatovic looked at some Boeing-owned buildings that didn't meet Safire's requirements. 

"In the meantime, the Wichita economic development people have supplied us information with respect to Mid-Continent Airport," Fatovic says. "They've also sent us some nice information about quality of life, the jet labor force, incentives that would be there, etc." 

Incentives at work 

Fatovic won't say what incentives Wichita offered, but an example of what might be possible can be found on the east side of Mid-Continent -- Cessna's new $61 million Citation Service Center. 

The 443,000-square-foot facility is nearing completion. Cessna plans to move 600 employees into the building around the first of the year and eventually add another 500 jobs. That's similar in size to Safire's planned final assembly complex. 

Allen Bell, director of economic development for the city of Wichita, says a combination of federal, state and local incentives persuaded Cessna to build the new service center at Mid-Continent. 

He says the incentive package is an excellent investment in the area's economy. 

"It's a major development and expansion of Cessna's presence here," Bell says. "It's a part of their operations, which are not subject to the periodic downturn of the aviation economy. And it brings in a lot of people to Wichita -- people who spend a lot of money while they're here." 

The Federal Aviation Administration, at the request of Rep. Todd Tiahrt (R-Goddard), spent $11 million for a new taxiway parallel to the east runway that will allow aircraft to taxi to the new facility. 

The Wichita Airport Authority matched the FAA grant money and helped finance construction with Airport Special Facility Revenue Bonds that Cessna will pay back. 

The company also has a 40-year lease for the land, which is exempt from property taxes because it's owned by the airport. 

The city spent $8.7 million to extend utilities to the site and for dirt work to raise the site's elevation to match the level of the taxiway. 

Sedgwick County and the state combined to rebuild Hoover Road north of K-42 to improve traffic flow into the facility. 

"We definitely thought outside the box," Bell says. "It's probably the high-water mark for the city stepping up for a business." 

There are two large land tracts on Mid-Continent property large enough for Safire's needs, and both have runway access. One site is along Tyler Road to the west of the airport's runways. The other is located on the southern end of the airport with access to K-42. 

In addition to incentives available through the airport authority, other eco/devo tools include tax credits for job training programs, industrial revenue bonds, enterprise zones, property tax abatement and forgivable loans. 

"Some of those are basically formula," says Patrick French, economic development director with the Greater Wichita Economic Development Coalition. "They are based upon the number of jobs that are created, based upon the average wages that are paid and based upon the capital investment." 

French says economic development officials are limited by state law on what they can offer to lure a company to Wichita or keep one from leaving. 

"The vast majority, both in terms of numbers of deals and dollar amounts of incentives provided, go to existing businesses that are expanding," Bell says. 

Local economic development officials know they don't work in a vacuum. Other cities want to land companies such as Safire because of the number of jobs the company will bring to their community. 

Most states offer incentives similar to the ones available in Kansas. Others go beyond. 

For example, New Mexico officials put together a package that included 150 acres of free land, IRBs, job training tax credits and tax abatements to lure Eclipse Aviation, another light business jet manufacturer, to Albuquerque. 

And recently, that state's legislature created a high wage jobs tax credit. 

For every job that pays a base salary of at least $40,000, the state provides a 10 percent tax credit on the combined value of the wage and benefits for each employee. 

"It is an incredible program that is winning us a great amount of attention from companies throughout the country," says Gary Tonjes, executive director of Albuquerque Economic Development Inc. 

Fatovic says Safire is evaluating information from Wichita along with sites in Florida, North Carolina, Virginia, Georgia, Alabama, Texas and Colorado. He says the decision should be announced by the end of June. 

"If you're looking at a site that's a 'green field' that you have to have a facility built, then you've got some lead time you've got to contend with," Fatovic says.

MAXWELL

Archive <http://www.sptimes.com/columns/maxwell.shtml> 
By BILL MAXWELL, Times Columnist  <mailto:maxwell@sptimes.com> 

© St. Petersburg Times
published February 2, 2003 

  _____  

In 1949, Virgil Hawkins, an African-American professor at historically black Bethune-Cookman College in Daytona Beach, applied for admission to the University of Florida College of Law. Hawkins' application was summarily rejected. And in in quick order, the state Board of Regents, the state attorney general and the Florida Supreme Court agreed that Hawkins could not attend UF's law school. 

In the court's last word on the matter -- flouting a U.S. Supreme Court decision -- Florida Supreme Court Justice Glenn Terrell, an unreconstructed racist, declared that racial segregation was God's wish for humankind: "When God created man, he created each race to his own continent according to color -- Europe to the white man, Africa to the black man, and America to the red man." 

For many African-Americans, as the hypocritical debate over affirmative action rages today, Terrell's words still resonate. We hear his warped attitude reflected in much of the right-wing talk about the evil of affirmative action for black citizens, a group that has been systematically and institutionally denied admission into many mainstream arenas while many unqualified whites enjoy admission. 

Hawkins and other aspiring black lawyers had nowhere to go if they wanted to learn their profession in their home state of Florida. Jim Crow ruled the day and was supported by segregationist readings of the Old Testament and racist interpretations of the Florida and U.S. constitutions. Later, without benefiting Hawkins and his generation, the U.S. Supreme Court outlawed discrimination based solely on skin color. 

Suddenly, officials at UF would have to admit blacks into its flagship, lily-white law school. UF and its supporters in Tallahassee were not ready to commit such an act of justice. What happened next, as described in the 2002 summer issue of The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education, gave Florida officials a way to maintain de facto segregation at UF: 

"[U]nder the separate but equal principle of Plessy vs. Ferguson, if the University of Florida was not willing to admit black students to its law school, the state would have to provide 'equal' facilities for blacks. So in 1951 a small law school was created on the campus of Florida A&M University in Tallahassee. It had a tiny 6,000-book library. Over the next 17 years, the law school graduated only 57 students, an average of less than four per year." 

But change marched into the Sunshine State. With Hawkins stepping aside, the state agreed to let other blacks into UF, and shrewd lawmakers immediately cut off funding to FAMU's law school. The 6,000-book collection was boxed up and carted off to the law library at Florida State University over the next hill. 

During subsequent years, blacks attended UF's law school, but their relationship with the college has been rocky at best, and reports of discrimination never go away. 

Now, with Republicans and their supporters demonizing affirmative action, Florida has fashioned a new, more benign, form of Jim Crow. And the precepts underpinning Plessy vs. Ferguson have given legislators a way to play all sides of the issue. 

Two years ago, Florida Gov. Jeb Bush issued an executive order banning race as a consideration in admission to the state's universities. He implemented the so-called One Florida plan, which was supposed to replace affirmative action. It admitted to the state university system the top 20 percent of the graduating class at each public high school. These otherwise qualified students, however, would have to compete for slots at the flagship UF campus. And, of course, race could not be a consideration. 

With the then-2002 gubernatorial election fast approaching, with black anger fomenting over One Florida and with black and Hispanic demands for new law schools growing louder, Bush reached into the past and gave them what they wanted. He and the GOP-controlled Legislature established law schools for mostly black FAMU and predominantly Hispanic Florida International University in Miami. 

Consider this contradictory language in the legislation authorizing FAMU's law school: "The college of law at Florida A&M University shall be dedicated to providing opportunities for minorities to attain representation with the legal profession proportionate to their representation in the general population. However, the college of law shall not include preferences in the admissions process for applicants on the basis of race, national origin, or sex." 

Fancy language aside, everyone knows that the FAMU law school -- a second-tier institution -- will become a virtual ghetto, while UF's law school will become whiter. 

Here is The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education's assessment of what FAMU's law school means: "Segregationists . . . were delighted with the prospect of a new law school earmarked for blacks. The legislators necessarily knew that very few white students would want to attend a law school at a historically black university. Like it or not, in the minds of most whites a continuing stigma attaches to black educational institutions. Therefore, it was almost certain that blacks would take up most of the spaces at the new school." 

Like many other Florida-based black journalists, I got to know Virgil Hawkins well. My sense is that even if FAMU's law school were created with the best of intentions, Hawkins would see it as a gussied-up version of Jim Crow. 

The unflattering truth is that FAMU's law school would have been Hawkins' second or third choice. Remember, he applied to the University of Florida, not to one of the nation's black colleges of law. He wanted to attend the state's best. 

Jeb Bush

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Subject: Cape Coral Municipal Charter High School

Governor Bush,

I'm sure you are aware that the City of Cape Coral began a municipal charter school system a couple of years ago.  I was in favor of the project while a member of the Cape Coral City Council and remained committed to it when my term expired last April.  I am still a member of the Charter School Board.

We opened our first elementary school last fall and will be opening another elementary school and a middle school this fall.  Our plans include building a charter high school on a beautiful piece of property that the City purchased for an Academic Village, which will house not only the charter high school, but also branch campuses of colleges and universities.  Because of our commitment to higher education, four colleges are now offering courses in Cape Coral in temporary quarters throughout the City, anticipating a move to the Academic Village where they can offer more programs.

Our plans to open the high school in 2007 may be seriously compromised because of delays in acquiring the required permits.  I wrote to President Bush last fall asking for assistance in expediting the process through the Army Corps of Engineers.  I received a response from the White House and a follow-up letter from the Corps stating that the project would be worked as quickly as possible.

However, our worst fears have now been realized because the permitting process has bogged down.  Unless we can acquire the permits within the next 2-3 months, the opening of the high school will be delayed, placing in jeopardy our commitment to provide a seamless transition for our students from kindergarten through high school.  The Army Corps of Engineers, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Agency and the Southwest Florida Water Management District are the three agencies involved in the permitting process.  The Corps is the lead agency on the project.

In addition to providing housing for a high school and various colleges and universities, the buildings at the Academic Village site will be "hardened" so that they can also serve as much needed hurricane shelters for our residents.  I should also mention that the Academic Village site is located in one of the highest and driest areas of the City.

My understanding is that there are no major problems with securing the permits.  The problem appears to be one of just moving the paperwork through the agencies that need to review it.

I am aware that the agencies charged with approving projects of this type are stretched to the limit and short-staffed.  However, this project will meet critical educational as well as public safety needs and is not a for profit venture.  Therefore, a timely completion of the project is vitally important to our community.

As you know better than anybody else, school districts across Florida are stretched to the limit as they try to meet the demand for a growing student population.  Lee County is no exception.  Therefore, if we are unable to open the high school in 2007, additional burdens will be placed on the Lee County School District that it may not be able to meet.

Therefore, all of those involved in this very worthwhile project would greatly appreciate anything you could do help us secure the permits so that our high school/hurricane shelter can be completed by August, 2007.  The Corps permit application number for the project is 2005-856.

Thank you.

Paul D. Asfour, Member
City of Cape Coral Municipal Charter School Board

To:	Jeb Bush
Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

melinda w sowder 7071 n mt tabor rd former 17 year resident ellettsville, in 47429 United States

From:	Yablonski, Brian <brian.yablonski@myflorida.com>
Sent:	Monday, July 23, 2001 11:55 AM
To:	'jeb@jeb.org'; Brogan, Frank; Arduin, Donna; Jimenez, Frank
Cc:	Shanahan, Kathleen; Oviedo, Nina; Hansen, Michael
Subject:	Health Team Trip to Washington

Last week, we met with members of the Bush Administration's
Medicaid/Medicare team and key Congressional staff involved with
Medicaid/Medicare reform on House and Senate side.  In addition, we met with
Speaker Hastert's top advisor on health policy issues.  Here's a brief
snapshot of findings.  Others on email may want to supplement if i've left
anything out.

On Medicaid Reform

Congress and the Administration are currently overwhelmed with Medicare
reform.  Medicaid issues will not take a front seat until the former is
completed.  However, with TANF reauthorization, they expect next year to be
the year for Medicaid issues.  

The Administration would rather do as much as it can in-house on Medicaid
first before going to Congress.  HHS is currently working on a Model
Medicaid Waiver -- they made clear that on waivers, HHS will grant the
greatest flexibility possible for innovation, but the initiatives must be
budget neutral. They also want better guidance from the states as to the
impacts of the waivers requested.  HHS will not predicate waivers based on
expansions.

As it relates to the NGA proposal as an option for reform (flexibility with
expansion), HHS made clear that they have a problem with what NGA proposed
and was well aware of our position, which they shared.  Mark McClellan, the
President's policy advisor on this, also agrees with our position -- they
are looking at Medicaid reform that would be based on "flexibility with
performance/accountability."  Using the same amount of funding to move in a
new direction.  We shared our position on the NGA proposal with all the Hill
staff that we met -- most seemed sympathetic and were skeptical that the NGA
proposal would get any traction based on budget realities.

We shared with them our views on Medicaid reform overall not displacing the
private insurance market, and adding more personal involvement and
responsibility to reforms much like welfare reform.  Both HHS and WH want
our specific input on the wavier and reform as this moves forward.  They
want ideas on how we show "performance."

On Medicare Reform

Everyone believes reform will happen this year -- with a bill emerging from
Congress in either October or November.  The House Energy and Commerce staff
assured us that all the proposals on the table right now have the federal
government fully picking up the cost of drugs for Medicaid/Medicare
dually-eligibles, which would amount to a $700 million fed/state savings
over time -- the over time is the key point here as the phase in is likely
to take a while.

There is also discussion on the Hill on Medicare reform adding some type of
means-testing component/looking at premium subsidies from the government to
be based on income.

On S-CHIP Coverage for Children of Immigrants

We made the pitch at a number of meetings and there is legislation currently
filed in Congress that would allow us to do this.  However, the proposal to
provide this coverage was met with some skepticism based on Congressional
dynamics.  We were told by Hill staff that the Speaker had some concerns
with the legislation and perceived it as a roll back on welfare reform
advances.  Mike did a good job stessing the importance of this to the
Speaker's aide and explaining why this was not rolling back the principles
of welfare reform -- part of Florida's allocation that we cannot draw
down/the "federal responsibility" for our borders and immigration.  All and
all, it was not a hopeful outlook.

On Florida Drug Formulary

Everyone in DC was interesting in our Pfizer agreement and how the formulary
works.  HHS did indicate that Pharma wants HHS to review our new law.  We
need to find a better way to package this initiative (pr-wise) for those who
are interested -- AHCA currently is passing out a powerpoint presentation
that they use, but its a little technical and not as comprehensive
Mike/Greg, can you work with Bob's shop/AHCA communications to have them
create a simple two/three pager that covers the major features of the law,
the agreement, how we are measuring performance, timing, efforts to move
forward.

On Nursing Home Initiative

HHS indicated they will be moving foward with some type of nursing home
quality initiative that is not all directly financial assistance, but would
have many components.  They were not in a position to share too many
details, but we did offer to have Florida be one of their showcase states --
based on our own reforms from this year.

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Riviera waterfront makeover uncertain 
By  <mailto:bill_cooper@pbpost.com> William Cooper Jr. 
Palm Beach Post Staff Writer 
Tuesday, May 09, 2006 
RIVIERA BEACH - For 10 months, city officials knew the battle over
eminent domain put its ambitious $2.4 billion waterfront redevelopment
in a political cross-fire in the Florida legislature.

When the dust finally settled last week, state lawmakers had struck a
near fatal blow when it passed a bill that strips cities like Riviera
Beach of the power to take land and give it to private developers.
Viking Inlet Harbor Properties, the city's master developer, was
counting on an amendment to protect Riviera Beach's right to use eminent
domain to turn about 400 acres of blight into a dazzling waterfront
community.

The setback highlights an ongoing power struggle between Mayor Michael
Brown, the self-proclaimed architect of International Harbor Village,
the city's redevelopment project, and the city council, which also sits
as the Community Redevelopment Agency board. Brown, an attorney who
practices eminent domain law, told the CRA board in February that the
city should start filing eminent domain proceedings before the
legislature took action in order to protect Riviera Beach's project.

That didn't happen. The CRA board promised residents that eminent domain
would only be used as a last resort in its effort to build a hotel,
shops, restaurants, marina, condos, an aquarium and a maritime charter
school along the Intracoastal Waterway.

Riviera Beach officials have been under intense pressure after a U.S.
Supreme Court decision regarding eminent domain shined the media
spotlight on the city's plan, which was promoted nationally to displace
about 5,100 people. Realistically, the figures are about 347 homeowners
and 1,000 renters being uprooted by the project.

Had the city filed the eminent domain actions in court, the
legislature's impact would be minimal, said Brown, who last September
won the right to return to the dais during CRA meetings after board
members ousted him, claiming he wasn't a legal member of the board.

His argument is supported when looking at Boynton Beach, where
redevelopment officials filed eminent domain cases weeks prior to the
bill passing, thus protecting their right to turn over the land to a
private developer.

"I think it would have been a good strategy," Brown said. "Had the city
taken the action this would have been water under the bridge."

Not necessarily, said City Council Chairwoman Ann Iles and Councilwoman
Liz Wade. Both believe that the project will work without eminent
domain.

"I don't think we have to use eminent domain," Iles said Friday. "Most
of the people who wanted to sell have sold and those who don't want to
sell, we have to do something else for them."

Wade doesn't see how the city could have started any eminent domain
actions given that the CRA is still negotiating its contract with
Viking. No specific property owners had been targeted as unwilling to
sell, she said.

From a political standpoint, Wade understands why legislators took such
a hard-line position. 
"You had a national outcry that was heard from coast to coast," Wade
said. "Legislatures across the country had to answer that cry. They had
to respond or none of them would be in office."

But Wade wants the legislature to compensate the city if Viking pulls
out of the deal and won't pay for $7 million in CRA bond anticipation
notes. The money is due to Wachovia Bank in July and Viking had agreed
to pay the debt once it signed a contract with the CRA. 

"The legislators are going to have to listen to us," she said, referring
to the cities throughout the state that have been adversely affected by
the legislation. "Maybe they can come back and clean up the
legislation."

Bob Healey, chairman of Viking Group, the lead company in Viking Inlet
Harbor Properties, said he and his team are assessing the damage. Viking
is slated to make a presentation about the project on Wednesday at the
regular CRA meeting.

"Can we go forward with parcels of it and shut down other parcels?"
asked Healey. "We've got to reassess the entire thing."

Healey and city officials believed Riviera Beach was out of the
political line of fire. They were able to get an amendment sponsored
that would have given them until 2010 before having to abide by the
eminent domain reforms.

But an 11th hour fight over school vouchers put the amendment on the
chopping block. It died a quick death in both House and Senate. 

Healey said his greatest fear has emerged. Land speculators are swooping
in and trying to buy as much of the land in the CRA area as possible.
Homeowners and businesses in the area are being peppered with mailings
from large real estate firms offering to buy their properties, said
Healey, whose business, Viking Yacht Co., is located in the CRA area and
has received such solicitations.

Without eminent domain, speculators will drive up land costs out of
sheer greed, he said. If the city wants to proceed under those
conditions, the price tag of the project will sky-rocket, he said.

But Frank Schnidman, a senior fellow at Florida Atlantic University's
Center for Urban and Environmental Solutions, said things in Riviera
Beach aren't as dire as they may look. For Schnidman, who is known
nationally for his urban planning work and filed a brief in the Supreme
Court case that set the eminent domain precedent, the project's
viability really boils down to one word: money.

"The developers are going to make less money," said Schnidman, who also
is executive director of the North Miami CRA. 
Schnidman has studied Riviera Beach's redevelopment plan and called it
one of the best in Florida. But the CRA and Viking must be willing to
make some financial concessions and take a more creative approach to the
project. The loss of eminent domain shouldn't kill Harbor Village, but
it now requires that the city make residents more like partners in the
deal instead of people who just have to get out of the developer's way.

"The power of eminent domain has made many redevelopment officials
lazy," Schnidman said. "It has taken away the opportunity for creative
thought."

Meanwhile, the real legal issue that Florida legislators should have
dealt with was accurately defining slum and blight, which are
cornerstones of eminent domain law, Schnidman said. Florida's loose
definition of blight has caused much of the abuse of eminent domain, he
said.

"It's made it easy to abandon poor people," he said. 
But in Martha Babson's case, the issue helped boost the value of her
home in the eyes of developers, while she criticized the city's
redevelopment plan. Babson gained national media attention as a
homeowner fighting to protect private property rights. 

While debate swelled, Babson eventually sold her quaint cottage near the
Intracoastal Waterway in January to developer Wayne Huizenga Jr. for
$732,000, more than three times its $202,454 appraised value.

Huizenga announced plans earlier this year to build a megayacht repair
facility near Babson's 21st Street home. The business is expected to add
100 jobs in the city.

Babson has always contended that Riviera Beach's assessment of the
blighted areas in the CRA was faulty. She even did her own examination
of the redevelopment area and challenged the city's blight study - a
review required by Florida law in order to use eminent domain.

Babson hopes the legislative reforms will make the city rethink its plan
and not just hand over some of the city's most precious land to a
private developer.

"We're all jumping up and down over here," said Babson, who is referring
to her neighbors, many whom also sold their land for lucrative sums. "I
think it's a wonderful challenge for Riviera Beach to start thinking in
a creative way."

Babson, however, won't be around to see it. She's moving to Gainesville
in the next year.

Dear Megan,

I am Governor Bush's chief lawyer. He received your email and asked if I
would respond for him. Your teacher has given you a very interesting
assignment and a very important one.

As you may have learned in school, there are three different branches to our
government. We have the executive (such as the Governor), the legislative
and the judicial (courts).  All three are independent from each other. The
legislature makes the laws. The Governor carries out the laws. The courts
interpret the laws -- that is, they tell us whether someone has acted in
accordance with the laws.

The judges who sit on the courts are independent. No one else can tell them
what to do. Some judges are elected and some are appointed by the Governor.
Even then, no one can tell them how to rule. This is a vital part of our
democracy.

This independence is important. In some cases, judges and juries (citizens
who help the judge decide the facts) decide whether people who are accused
of a crime are guilty or innocent. Since no one can tell them what to do,
their only obligation is to follow the laws that the legislature enacted and
the constitution that the citizens approved.  This protects the liberty of
the accused, who cannot go to jail unless the government proves its case
under the law. 

If courts were not independent, like in a dictatorship, the government could
send anyone they wanted to jail, whether or not they broke the law. That
would be horrible.

It is important that courts protect their independence by respecting their
role. Since they are not legislators, they are not there to make up the law.
They are there to follow it. If they made up the law any way they wanted,
then this would hurt our liberties, because we never would know when a court
would say we were right or wrong. It would be like your parents changing the
rules all the time and just punishing you whenever they wanted.

I hope that this will help you in your school assignment. I am sure that
Governor Bush would enjoy reading your paper. You can email it to me, and I
will send it to him.

Good luck!

Officer Is Punished For Taser Incidents

Michael Branch is suspended 29 hours without pay for shocking students.

By DANA WILLHOIT

The Ledger

LAKELAND -- When some Lakeland High School baseball players asked the school resource officer to shoot them with his Taser, the officer complied.

The boys told the officer they wanted to know how it felt.

Officer Michael Branch got his thanks Friday when he was suspended from duty for using the weapon on five players.

"You had no permission or authority to use your Taser in this fashion," Lakeland Police Chief Roger Boatner wrote to Branch in a disciplinary letter released Friday. "You are not a certified Taser instructor."

The Taser is used to temporarily disable a suspect with a powerful electrical charge. The weapon is widely used by police departments around the country as an alternative to guns.

Branch, a Lakeland police officer since 1988, was suspended without pay for 29 hours after an internal affairs investigation found he inappropriately used his Taser on high school students on two occasions.

The first was in December and involved the baseball players.

In the second, on Jan. 12, Branch "tased" two students who were watching a fight.

Branch was pushing his way through a crowd of students when he saw a teacher trying to break up the fight get knocked over. According to LPD spokesman Jack Gillen, Branch said he told the two students to get out of his way, and they ignored him.

But the students both told police Branch didn't say anything to them before shocking them with the Taser.

"The students were not facing you at the time and did not offer active physical resistance," Boatner said in his disciplinary letter to Branch.

Soladaye Oyelowo, 17, one of the students who was shocked, complained to the Police Department.

"The student believes that you should have apologized. He told Internal Affairs, `If he would've just apologized, I would have been, you know, I wouldn't have got upset or nothing,' " Boatner told Branch in his letter.

But Oyelowo's mother, Theodora Oyelowo, was furious.

She told The Ledger at the time that she wasn't aware Tasers were used at the high school. She filed a complaint against Branch the day after the incident.

But the parents of Chris Sale, one of the baseball players, had a different take on the situation.

"I like Officer Branch, and that's all I have to say about it," Sale's mother, Marla Sale, a former Lakeland police dispatcher, said Friday.

Sale's father, Allen Sale, said he heard about the incident from boys on the baseball team the night it happened.

"They were laughing about it. I laughed with them," Sale said.

Chris Sale, in fact, said that the Taser wasn't any big deal and asked Branch to do it a second time, his father said. Branch turned up the voltage and shocked him again, and the boy ended up "flopping around like a fish on the sidewalk," his father said.

Branch has since been transferred to Lakeland Highlands Middle School, where he works as that school's resource officer.

"I hate, hate, hate that he's not at Lakeland High School any more," Allen Sale said.

Lakeland High Principal Mark Thomas said Branch did a good job at the school up until the Taser incidents.

Thomas said that Tasers are serious weapons and should be respected as such.

The officer came to LHS about midyear last year, Thomas said.

Branch, 43, who voluntarily gave up his Taser, has worked as a school resource officer for five years.

He makes $51,914 a year, according to Gillen. Branch was suspended for 21 hours for the baseball player incident and eight hours for the second.

However, because the internal affairs investigators felt there were "mitigating circumstances" during the second incident, the eight-hour suspension will run concurrent with the first -meaning Branch only loses 21 hours of pay, amounting to about $524.

Alessandra Meetz, a spokeswoman for the ACLU of Florida, said the civil liberties group is concerned about the use of Tasers in high schools.

"They should be dictated by necessity," she said. "They're supposed to be used in cases where, otherwise, the police would use lethal force. They become problematic and dangerous when used in situations where no one would use lethal force."

Tasers use compressed nitrogen to shoot two small, electrified probes as far as 21 feet. The probes stick in the body, transmitting as much as 50,000 volts of electricity.

Tasers can also be deployed without the cartridge attached. That's how Branch used it on the students on both occasions.

In those situations, the Taser is pressed directly against a target's body and activated.

Around the country, a number of people have died after being shot with Tasers, including a 32year-old Polk County man last summer.

The Polk County Medical Examiner's Office determined that the death of Jason Yeagley of Auburndale was not caused by the Taser fired by a Polk County deputy.

Yeagley died from "excited delirium" due to withdrawal from the prescription drug Xanax, the Medical Examiner's Office concluded.

Broward sheriff predicts problems with `force with force' law
  
By Ken Kaye, Staff Writer

April 7, 2005

Weston . Broward Sheriff Ken Jenne on Wednesday chastised the proposed "meet force with force" bill, saying it could lead to accidental shootings and puts too much discretion in the hands of residents rather than law enforcement officials.

"Some interpretations of the law go beyond what I think communities want," Jenne said at a meeting of Weston residents and homeowner association presidents.

The measure would allow a person under attack to use deadly force without retreating, whether he or she is at home, on the street or in a bar. The National Rifle Association strongly endorses the bill, and Gov. Jeb Bush plans to sign it into law.

But Jenne said such a law might inspire people to fire guns needlessly and with tragic consequences.

For instance, he said if a parent were chasing a child down the street, and a neighbor thought the child was in danger, the neighbor could shoot at the parent.

Or, he said, if a thief steals a woman's purse and flees, the victim could fire a long-range weapon at the culprit, as long as he still is within a three-block range. Stealing a purse doesn't warrant shooting to kill, Jenne said.

"I don't think that is what a community needs," Jenne said. "It's easy after the fact to say, `I felt threatened.'"

Jenne said police, not residents, are best suited to draw weapons because they would exercise proper judgment. Just the same, if the bill is approved, "we'll enforce the law," he said.

Also at meeting, held jointly by the Bonaventure Presidents' Council and the Weston Council of Presidents, Jenne assured that his department is working to stamp out identity theft and juvenile speeding, two areas that have become increasingly troublesome in Weston and countywide.

Motorists can expect to see more motorcycle officers holding speed-monitoring laser guns because speeding and running red lights account for the majority of road deaths in this county, Jenne said.

The laser guns, he said, are "accurate, accepted in court and they can catch a speeder 1,800 feet away."

Identify theft thieves, who go through people's garbage and mail to find credit card numbers and other financial information, reap $300,000 to $400,000 a year, Jenne said. He said the Broward Sheriff's Office is working with the FBI and the Secret Service to stem the crime.

"I'm telling you it's a major fraud that's going to spread more day after day," he said.

Responding to a question, Jenne also admitted his department made errors to clear crimes, which has resulted in a State Attorney's Office investigation into whether reports were falsified.

But he said the Sheriff's Office has made 22 policy changes to ensure the errors aren't repeated, including officers being required to record "exceptional clearances" on video.

"We recognized there was a problem, and we're doing business a whole different way," he said.

From: Your Voice [ mailto:YourVoice@MyFlorida.Com] 
Sent: Wednesday, January 31, 2001 7:20 PM 
To: Your Voice 
Subject: Modernizing Our State Workforce 

Dear Colleague: 

As Governor, I have always considered it an honor and a privilege to lead 
such a hardworking group of men and women in providing services to our 
citizens.  The talents, dedication and commitment our state employees show 
on a daily basis continue to leave me both humbled and proud.  As public 
employees, in many ways, you have helped to make Florida a model state, and 
I believe we should build on your accomplishments by continuing to find ways 
to better serve Floridians.  

When I announced my budget recommendations earlier this month, I stated that 
the old way of doing something is not necessarily the best way to go about 
our business.  Recently, the Council of 100, a bipartisan cross section of 
key business leaders from around the state, issued a report encouraging 
state government to revisit and modernize its state personnel system.  In 
response to some of their ideas, I am encouraging key policymakers to review 
and make reform suggestions for our career service and state personnel 
system.  I want to take this opportunity to share with you my own vision of 
this reform, and more importantly, to ask for your assistance and input.  

First, I hope that any reform effort foremost places a priority on merit. 
That was the original intent of the career service system.  Like the rest of 
Florida's not for profit organizations and private sector businesses, 
demonstration of your initiative and ability should count for something in 
determining compensation, pay raises, and promotions.  Today, however, much 
of our effort to recognize employees is done "across the board" with little 
means for singling out hard work and accomplishment.  Reform should lead to 
a system where the achievement of performance criteria translates into 
special bonuses and incentives.  

Second, I believe in giving employees greater choices.  State government, 
through the various forms of leave and benefits offered, should allow you 
the flexibility to manage your resources.  One reform idea for consideration 
is the option of being allowed to cash out on your unused leave balance at 
the end of each cycle rather than having it continue to roll over year after 
year. 

Third, employees, especially employees who perform well, should be better 
compensated.  Agency managers and supervisors should be given more freedom 
to direct unused salary to good employees.  Our state budget recommendations 
for fiscal year 2001/2002 provide for a $158 million increase in pay over 
last year, including bonuses for performance.  If the Legislature embraces 
these recommendations, many employees will see their annual paycheck 
increase by as much as five percent or more.  As well, building on the 
concept of the Davis Productivity Awards, there should be greater financial 
incentives for employees who generate ideas that result in a savings to the 
taxpayers of Florida. 

Fourth, reforms should continue to protect workers against discrimination 
and patronage.  Career service workers should not be concerned about their 
political party affiliation or their age, race or gender.  These are all 
basic rights that should not be abridged.  

Fifth, I believe in a state personnel system where employment is objectively 
based on sustained performance and fitness for public service, instead of 
arbitrarily based on tenure and seniority.  No one should be given an unfair 
advantage over another, especially without regard to performance. 

And finally, our processes and practices need to be streamlined in order to 
more efficiently respond to taxpayers and the needs of the state. 
Classification systems should be simplified, hiring processes should give 
agencies the ability to act within a reasonable period of time, and 
grievance resolution processes should provide for fair and efficient due 
process.  

In short, a vision for reform should be one that provides a dynamic career 
service system where hard work, performance and achievement are recognized; 
where employees still have basic protections; and where merit, not time 
served, is the final arbiter of success. 

There is much to be done, and I would like your thoughts and suggestions on 
career service reform.  Are there particular areas of the state employment 
system where we should be focused?  Do you have any personal experiences 
that would be helpful in developing reforms?  How should bonuses be 
allocated within an agency to ensure we are rewarding performance?  I have 
asked our Secretary of the Department of Management Services, Cynthia 
Henderson and Secretary of the Department of the Lottery, David Griffin to 
work with the Legislature to develop a reform initiative.  In addition, in 
early February, our agency heads will be setting up informal employee 
outreach sessions to solicit your input and feedback on the career service 
system and state personnel system.  In the meantime, please email us with 
your own ideas on state personnel system reform at yourvoice@myflorida.com 
< mailto:yourvoice@myflorida.com>.   

Best wishes in this New Year, and I look forward to hearing from you. 

                                            Sincerely, 

                                            Jeb Bush

Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Karen Duff 3230 New England Lane Export, PA 15632 United States
