	Boxer pledges shift on global warming policy with new Senate role

	SAMANTHA YOUNG

	Associated Press

	SACRAMENTO, Calif. - Sen. Barbara Boxer on Thursday promised major
policy shifts on global warming, air quality and toxic-waste cleanup as she
prepares to head the U.S. Senate's environmental committee.

	"Time is running out, and we need to move forward on this," Boxer
said of global warming during a conference call with reporters. "The states
are beginning to take steps, and we need to take steps as well."

	Boxer's elevation to chairwoman of the Senate Environmental Public
Works Committee comes as the Democrats return to power in the Senate. It also
marks a dramatic shift in ideology for the panel.

	The California Democrat is one of the Senate's most liberal members
and replaces one of the most conservative senators, Republican James Inhofe
of Oklahoma. Inhofe had blocked bills seeking to cut the greenhouse gases
contributing to global warming, calling the issue "the greatest hoax
perpetrated on the American people."

	Environmentalists were overjoyed at the change.

	"That's like a tsunami hit the committee," said Karen Steuer, who
heads government affairs at the National Environmental Trust, a nonprofit
based in Washington, D.C. "You can't find two members or people more
ideologically different.

	As chairman, Inhofe tried to overhaul the Endangered Species Act and
supported the Bush administration's 2002 rules to roll back provisions in the
Clean Air Act. He also promoted legislation that would have allowed the
government to suspend air quality and water quality rules in response to
Hurricane Katrina.

	It's a record that earned Inhofe the lowest possible legislative
score from the League of Conservation Voters. By comparison, Boxer, who has
made the environment a signature issue since coming to the Senate in 1992,
received a 93 percent rating.

	Boxer said she intends to introduce legislation to curb greenhouse
gases, strengthen environmental laws regarding public health and hold
oversight hearings on federal plans to clean up Superfund sites across the
country.

	On global warming, Boxer said she would model federal legislation
after a California law signed this summer by Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger. That
law imposes the first statewide cap on greenhouse gases and seeks to cut
California's emissions by 25 percent, dropping them to 1990 levels by 2020.

	"Some of the practical solutions are in the California approach,"
Boxer said.

	A top environmental aide at the White House signaled Thursday that
the administration would work with her.

	In an e-mail to the senator's chief counsel, George Banks, the
associate director for international affairs at the Council for Environmental
Quality requested a meeting to discuss global warming, Boxer said.

	President Bush has opposed a federal mandate to limit greenhouse gas
emissions from industry and automobiles, saying such steps should be
voluntary. His administration also has ruled that greenhouse emissions are
not a pollutant.

	"We look forward to working with Congress in bipartisanship on all
issues," said Kristen Hellmer, a spokeswoman for the Council on Environmental
Quality.

	She declined to discuss specifics related to the upcoming global
warming discussion.

	Democrats and environmentalists have criticized Bush for refusing to
send the Senate the 1997 Kyoto accord for ratification. It requires 35
industrialized countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 5 percent
below 1990 levels by 2012.

	California's law and various bills in Congress set more aggressive
targets.

	Whether Bush will consider reversing his long-standing policy of
making cutbacks in greenhouse gas emissions voluntary rather than mandatory
will be one test of the new reality he confronts Washington.

	The administration is defending a previous Environmental Protection
Agency ruling that greenhouse gases are not a pollutant under the Clean Air
Act. An appeal of that administrative rule is scheduled to go before the U.S.
Supreme Court later this month.

	California also is seeking a waiver to the Clean Air Act so it can
implement a law that took effect in 2004 forcing the auto industry to make
cleaner-burning vehicles. Automakers have sued in federal court to block the
California emissions law.

	"On the issue of global warming in particular, we're going to need a
new president before we see major progress," said Eric Antebi, spokesman for
the San Francisco-based Sierra Club. "But this Congress can really lay the
groundwork for that and make incremental changes."

	Boxer suggested she would push for energy-efficiency and
alternative-fuel programs that already have been adopted by dozens of states.

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

CONDO OWNERS PLEA FOR HELP, AS SENATE TRASHES BILL
Posted April 24, 2004 - 19:45 EST
 
MIAMI BEACH, FL -- Owners of condominiums gathered today in support of a legislative reform that would permit a state Ombudsman to investigate cases of fraud and illegal activity.
 
State Representative Julio Robaina (R-117), who introduced what has been nicknamed,  "The Condo Owners' Bill of Rights", officially known as HB 1223, was welcomed with a standing ovation by those who attended

There was a clear show of support for this new bill amongst those present.
 
Eddie Hernandez, unit owner of a condominium in Hialeah Gardens spoke about the troubles when he reported his association board members to the law enforcement agencies.
 
"I wrote Diane Carr, Secretary of the Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) but never got a response from her.", Hernandez indicated.
 
The DBPR, which is responsible for overseeing the problems and enforcing the laws at condominiums, enjoyed very little support from those present.
 
JoAnn Weissman wrote the DBPR with complaints of her condominium board and all she obtained was a letter, which promised to investigate.

Robaina's bill was tranformed into a spineless piece of legislation that would benefit no one or nothing, but instead maintains the status-quo
 
Carr, who has thus far proven to be ineffective and unresponsive to unit owners, would now appoint and oversee the ombudsman.

I ask this only as a point of information (not in criticism---I know the state always has finite preservation funds) at this time because, as you may be aware, Orange County is cooking up this "tech corridor" called Innovation Way which, if realized, will be tantamount to an incendiary bomb dropped upon the most ecologically sensitive and varigated & hydrologically vital swath in east central Florida.  The interdependent interconnectivity of the natural communities is so intricate and so tight-knit that it is, and I know biologists will attest to this, extremely difficult to develop in, on and around on a grand scale without severe disruption if not destruction of the natural system.  Yet Orange County proposes to do this, to the tune of a commercial/residential hub the size of the city of Orlando, precisely superimposed on this ecological trove. As example, the long ago-approved International Corporate Park destroyed a huge rcw cluster w/take and failed relocations, and has NUMEROUS listed species hanging in the balance of its development (including likely 1000 tortoises). IF piecemeal FWC permitting is the only "protection" our wildlife will have in Innovation Way, then we can kiss every living thing in the crosshairs of IW planners goodbye. It doesn't have to be so catastrophic if enough will and cooperation and expertise are in place to accomplish the appropriate land purchases and genuinely survey & protect the listed wildlife. We can have development AND keep the living web intact:  if it is done right.
 
So I'm looking for ways to help make sure there are real protections for wildlife and enough meaningful blocks of this Econ treasure saved so that the whole system doesn't wither and die from overzealous vivisection and amputation (similar, on a larger scale, to my arguments in the UCF NW Quadrant natural system requisite "intactness" before the whole thing falls apart, or fails, because it has met an inflexible threshold of what human incursion it can bear.)
 
Orange County, in its planning presentations to the public, says conservation and slowing sprawl are major driving components (besides the obvious "diversify-the-economy" ) behind Innovation Way. And indeed, every poll taken of the public's priorities showed an unambiguous plea for preservation/the environment/wildlife & habitat protection (no citizen pleas for more housing developments, note).  Yet the County has been almost absurdly vague about just how any species will actually get saved or key lands protected, because there is no effective mechanism in place to do so, and no specific data shown us about species in the tech corridor's path (or how the county plans to protect it) so that ANYONE---we, the people or even the approving agencies---can tell exactly what it is we are commenting on or approving.
 
Yet, the general blueprint, I think, will be up for transmittal (to DCA)approval Dec. 15th., painted with a brush as broad as the side of a barn.
 
My question to you is:  can the State, at least going forward, to some extent, in the near future, consider the Econ Basin as an area requiring some state scrutiny and preservation dollars, to, if nothing else, help ensure that this entire slice of our natural native legacy and HUGE chunk of tortoises and wildlife of regional/state significance won't be rubbed from the earth?
 
Could DEP/ARC work with the county on land purchases---even easements? Can they now get some dialogue w/Deseret? OF COURSE, now that Innovation Way has been announced, all the big ranch interests (including Deseret & Holland/TCM) are jumping up and declaring plans for high density housing developments to "accomodate the tech jobs" (jobs which as of now are imaginary) to the effect that land prices in the IW area will soar even more beyond the county's reach to purchase for preservation at their lowball appraisal prices, the self-fulfilling prophecy being:  oops, we can't afford to buy anything, nobody wants to sell for preservation because everybody wants on the bandwagon of housing development, where the big money is.
 
SO:  the "sprawl" claimed to be staved off by this projected magical economic boon, Innovation Way, will be WORSE than business as usual, and accelerated beyond belief, and down the road we won't have any living Econlockhatchee river, much less the torties, fox squirrels, panther, red-cockaded woodpeckers, celestial lilies et al that thrive there now and that we EXISTING residents hold dear.
 
Will the state keep the Econ on its radar screen?  (Please please please????) Can SOME of the tax windfall drift to Fl. Forever coffers earmarked "The Econ Mosaic"? The County just doesn't seem to have it together to really save anything---and that is my biggest fear.
 
Thanks for considering our neck of the woods.
 
Best Regards, and truly, a Happy Thanksgiving,
 
Rebecca

Accessible polls
Counties falling short of aid for disabled voters
By Nancy Cook Lauer
DEMOCRAT CAPITOL BUREAU CHIEF

Disabled voters should find polling places easier to get into come Election Day 2004. But they may not find it any easier to vote once they're there.

That's because a 2002 state law mandating at least one disabled-accessible voting machine per precinct was made contingent upon money being available - and a federal mandate requiring the machines doesn't kick in until 2006.

The problem is compounded by the fact that the state has yet to complete the complex certification process that will allow Diebold Election Systems - which holds contracts for optical-scan voting equipment in 30 of the state's 67 counties - to provide audio-capable touch-screen systems for the visually impaired.

Many counties using other optical-scan and touch-screen systems have purchased audio-capable machines that are used in a central location, but all counties fall far short of meeting the new precinct mandates.

"I expect we'll meet the 2006 deadline," said Doug Towne, president of the Florida Coalition for Disability Rights. "But many counties are still going through the motions."

It's an important issue. Almost 25 percent of the state's voting-age population has some kind of disability, and fully 40 percent of them went to the polls in the 2000 election, according to the American Association of People with Disabilities.

Towne, who lives in Pinellas County, had his first chance to vote on the audio machine in the 2002 election. He said he felt a new freedom - even though he actually was exercising what should have been a basic civil right to a secret ballot.

"I guess it's hard for sighted people to understand how it feels to vote for the first time without people helping you or kibitzing about who you vote for," Towne said.

Challenged in court

Some disabled-rights groups have lost patience with the process. Lawsuits filed in Palm Beach and Duval counties pushed for audio-capable voting machines in time for the 2002 election.

Last month a federal magistrate threw out the Palm Beach County case, which was filed by blind voters who wanted access to an audio-balloting machine in every precinct in the 2002 election. The magistrate noted that Elections Supervisor Theresa LePore has since provided machines.

A federal judge in Jacksonville is expected to rule soon on a similar lawsuit in Duval County, following a 6½-day trial in September. That suit was filed by the American Association of People with Disabilities, who contend the county was required to put in the accessible machines under the Americans With Disabilities Act when it upgraded from a punch-card to an optical-scan system.

Disabled advocates say the ADA requires all new government facilities to be accessible to the disabled when implemented, regardless of the provisions of the other federal mandate, the Help America Vote Act, known as HAVA.

"You can't open a new government building one year and say 'I'll put the elevator in next year. Until then, use the stairs'," said James Dickson, vice president of governmental affairs for the national group for the disabled.

Jacksonville was one of three cities targeted by national disabled advocates. The aim is to set a legal precedent that the ADA must be complied with on voting issues, Dickson said. Lawsuits filed in Philadelphia and Washington, D.C., by the National Organization on Disability have since been settled, with disabled advocates declaring victory.

An attorney in the Duval County case said the county had been prepared to offer three machines - they just hadn't been certified by the state Division of Elections in time. The Diebold machines still aren't certified and are undergoing another round of testing this week.

"The irony is we had every expectation that the disabled component would be certified, and the fact that it hasn't been has been a surprise to everybody," said Jacksonville Senior Assistant General Counsel Ernst Mueller, one of three attorneys defending the case.

Time-consuming process

Florida has some of the most rigorous certification standards for election equipment in the nation. State election officials say the cumbersome process is needed to ensure accuracy in balloting and counting votes. It's not unusual for it to take a year or more, they said.

"The Department of State reviews the vendor's application for completeness, establishes a qualification test plan and conducts a series of fundamental testing to ensure the system meets the minimum requirements of the Florida Voting System Standards and can properly support the conduct of a Florida election," said Secretary of State Glenda Hood. "We are confident the necessary procedures in place will continue our commitment to improve Florida's elections process, so all registered voters in Florida are able to cast their vote with confidence."

That's not fast enough for some disabled voters.

"Florida has a reputation of having one of the slowest certification processes there is," Dickson said. "Certainly we want slow, thorough and deliberate. But there's a difference between slow, thorough and deliberate and dawdling."

Election supervisors, have, however, made great strides trying to bring the polling locations themselves to compliance with the Americans With Disabilities Act.

County workers across the state spent the summer measuring parking spaces and curb heights at polling places. They tugged on doors with fish scales to determine how hard they are to open. They measured and counted handicapped parking spaces and combed through thousands of polling places to see where they needed updating.

Each county had to submit a 32-page accessibility survey to the state by Oct. 1. The state Division of Elections still is compiling the information, said a spokeswoman there.

Compliance won't be cheap.

Churches, often used for polling places because they are convenient to communities, are exempt from the ADA so they must be upgraded to meet polling-place requirements. Schools, another popular polling place, are in shorter supply as an unintended consequence of the constitutional amendment voters passed last year requiring smaller classrooms.

Deborah Clark, Pinellas County supervisor of elections, puts the cost of ADA compliance in her 302 polling places at about $800,000.

"What if we invest the money, and that location doesn't want to be a polling place anymore," she said. "This may drive us to regional polling places."

Leon County Supervisor of Elections Ion Sancho said it will cost the same $800,000 to put one audio balloting system in each of Leon's 126 polling places. Sancho chafed at White House delays in putting a committee together to implement HAVA and at uncertainty in Congress about how much money will be sent to states.

"Talk is cheap. But where is the money?" he asked.

Towne finds the money argument unacceptable.

"Nobody said that a constitutional government was cheap," Towne said. "If we want to make it cheaper, why don't we just do away with elections?"

FROM THE CHEAP SEATS: JERRY GREENE 
Gov. Bush blitzes in defense of FSU 
Jerry Greene
FROM THE CHEAP SEATS

August 9, 2005

Florida Governor Jeb Bush visited us Monday to play a little "Madden NFL 06" with its creators at EA Tiburon in Maitland. But while he was there, he expressed some hard-hitting views on what's really going on in Florida sports. We'll get back to Tiburon's virtual form of reality in a moment, but first . . .

Gov. Bush executed a perfect blindside blitz of the NCAA when he spoke out in vigorous defense of Florida State University's use of the nickname Seminoles despite recent NCAA actions to curb that use. Bush described the NCAA decisions as "ludicrous."

"I support [FSU] President T.K. Wetherell completely," Gov. Bush said at the conclusion of his visit. "It [the recent NCAA ruling] is ludicrous. They need to get out more."

The NCAA banned the use of American Indian nicknames and mascots by 18 college sports teams during postseason tournaments (not counting Division I football) beginning Feb. 1, 2006. Perhaps the most prominent is Florida State, where Wetherell was outraged at the accusations that use of such nicknames and mascots is "hostile and abusive."

"FSU's use of the word 'Seminoles' and its mascot, Chief Osceola, is not offensive to anybody, particularly the Seminoles of this state," Gov. Bush said. "You would have thought they [the NCAA] would have asked the people involved, but apparently not."

Bush pointed out that no changes are planned until early next year so "maybe reason will prevail."

And now we return to our regular programming . . .

The Gov pancakes the Prez

Gov. Bush was getting a brief introduction into the video-gaming universe of EA Tiburon when co-founder Steve Chiang unveiled a surprise gift. There on the big screen was Miami Dolphins wide receiver Jeb Bush breaking for the end zone with only one man in his way -- Dallas Cowboys defensive back George W. Bush.

Big Jeb ran over George W. like the Prez was Deion Sanders -- and the real Jeb Bush clearly loved watching. A copy of that special "Madden NFL 06" is on its way to the Presidential ranch in Crawford, Texas, as we speak.

The young wizards at Tiburon could have a new cottage industry by making special versions of "Madden NFL 06" that included the faces of famous people (or perhaps the face of your boss).

I can think of so many "defensive backs" that I'd love to trample.

After beating the Prez, Gov. Bush spoke to a room filled with young Tiburon employees. Hard to say why they were in the room. Maybe to see what a governor looked like or maybe for the free cookies. Maybe both.

Sounding pumped, the Governor praised Tiburon's value to the state and particularly Central Florida. This was the perfect location because, he said, "Florida has the best high school football by far." Everybody cheered.

Then he said Florida "has the best college football by far." Everybody cheered except for the UCF grads.

Then he started to say Florida has the best pro football by far -- and thought better of it.

No doubt he had a good time. But while he was talking to the young Tiburon crowd in their T-shirts and flip flops, I couldn't help but suspect Gov. Bush had to be thinking, "There's not a registered voter in the bunch."

Scalp 'em, FSU?

Gov. Bush should be applauded for his stance on Florida State's use of Seminoles. But that doesn't mean the situation can't be improved.

During Monday morning's session of the critically acclaimed Keep'n Score show on 740 the Team, we talked with Gene Deckerhoff, radio "voice" of FSU athletics and possibly the most fervent FSU Seminole alive. During the chat, he mentioned two interesting things:

The lyrics to the FSU fight song, written in the 1950s, contain the term "scalp 'em." In fact, here are the first two lines:

"You gotta fight fight fight for FSU!

You gotta scalp 'em, Seminoles!"

It wouldn't hurt for FSU (not the NCAA) to consider changing the "scalp 'em" to a simple "beat 'em." Actually, it wouldn't hurt to blow up the song for artistic reasons, but that's just my opinion.

Deckerhoff also mentioned that up until about two years ago, FSU Coach Bobby Bowden signed his autographs with "Scalp 'em!" and his signature. He no longer does that, which seems wise.

Football Countdown: 23 days

Easiest number to talk about in sports because Michael Jordan wore it during his glory years with the Chicago Bulls. He also briefly wore No. 45 after his first un-retirement. And surely you remember the one night he wore No. 12? Right here for a game with the Magic after someone stole his jersey.

No, none of this has anything to do with football. But you know what the countdown is all about. Closer and closer.

Nobody asked but still . . .

That "whooshing" sound you heard Monday was all the air going out of the 2005 hopes for Tampa Bay Bucs fans when they learned "Turnstile" Todd Steussie was back on the team -- and at left tackle now. Tip to Brian Griese: Make sure your papers are in order and you've said "goodbye" to your loved ones.

In related news: The Real Madrid soccer team has turned down more than 300 requests from the families of fans who wanted their ashes scattered inside the club's stadium. You're not thinking, Real Madrid. You can make a lot of families happy -- and save on fertilizer, too.

Sun Sports is repeating a special "Sports Talk Live" from Monday night that focused on the FSU/NCAA controversy. It airs today at 10 a.m., 6 p.m. and 11 p.m.

Considering the problems Lynx is having with getting paid for advertising, this probably is a bad time to make my annual push to get my face on the side of a bus, huh?

It's just wrong: You spent more than $30 million last weekend to watch The Dukes of Hazzard. And we know who you are.

New Vikings owner Zygmunt Wilf came to Orlando recently to talk to Daunte Culpepper about a contract adjustment. Culpepper got the adjustment but his contract still doesn't touch what Peyton Manning and Mike Vick have.

Whatever happened to the Fabulous Sports Babe?

Closing thought: "I never drink water because of the disgusting things that fish do in it." -- W.C. Fields.

Sent:	Friday, June 25, 2004 8:46 PM
To:	Jeb Bush
Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Matias is the kind of high school senior every university wants. He scored a 1290 on his SAT and has an A average. When he graduates in May, he will have eight to 12 college credits under his belt as a result of dual enrollment in college courses.

But Matias, who didn't want his full name used for fear of being deported to Argentina, probably won't attend college. He can't afford to.

As an undocumented immigrant, he must pay out-of state tuition -- $15,420 a year -- even though he has lived in South Florida for more than four years and will graduate with honors from a Florida high school. If he were here legally, in-state tuition would be a more manageable $2,913 at his school of choice, Florida International University.

''My parents can't afford out-of-state tuition,'' he says. ``Even if I got a job that would pay that much -- and I can't get a real job, either -- when would I have time to go to school? All I want to do is get an education and improve myself.''

Matias' dilemma is not unusual. Researchers estimate that as many as 2,000 Florida high school graduates who want to go to college are shut out every year by the high price Florida state schools charge undocumented immigrants. About two-thirds of those are in South Florida.

For the third year in a row, a bill has been filed in the Legislature that would allow Florida high school graduates without legal residency who have been in the country for at least three years to attend community colleges and universities at the resident rate.

Although the number of students that would be affected is small, the proposal is not a sure thing. Not at a time when college tuition costs are rising, the number of college-age students is growing, and state universities can be increasingly choosy about whom they admit.

Some parents worried about their own children's academic futures could take a dim view of lawmakers voting what amounts to a subsidy -- in-state tuition doesn't cover the cost of a college education -- to undocumented immigrants. Some opponents fear it could serve as an incentive, drawing more illegal immigrants to the state.

In the Senate, with a week left in the session, the legislation is still waiting to be scheduled on the Appropriations Committee calendar. In the House, it has been referred to the floor for a vote but no date has been set. The past two years, champions of these students have introduced similar legislation, only to see it die at the end of the sessions.

''We're talking about kids who have lived in this community for years and years, and they have become part of the community and lived by the rules,'' said Sen. Frederica Wilson, a Miami Democrat, one of the Senate sponsors. ``Now we tell them that they're no longer one of us and all the work they did to get through school doesn't count.''

OTHER STATES

Nine states -- Oklahoma, Utah, Texas, New York, California, Illinois, Washington and Kansas -- have laws that allow undocumented resident students to pay the same tuition rate as other state high school graduates. Florida is the only large state with a sizable immigrant population that charges these students out-of-state tuition.

Both Wilson and House sponsor Juan Zapata, R-West Kendall, see this as an issue of economics: A better-educated work force means more money in the economy, contributed by people with higher-paying jobs.

The two note that students who would qualify under this law have lived here for years and the state has already invested in their education. Most arrived as young children with their parents.

Under current immigration law, young people who are brought illegally to the United States by their parents or whose families overstay tourist visas have few avenues to ever gain legal U.S. residency. Federal measures to offer students who go to college or join the military a chance to gain legal residency have been stalled in Congress for almost two years.

Anielle, 19, came to South Florida with her parents from Haiti when she was a child. She took lots of science courses at Boyd Anderson High School in Fort Lauderdale, hoping to be a doctor. But her education ended last year when she graduated, because her family can't afford to pay out-of-state tuition.

Last March she went with a group of students to Tallahassee to speak at a rally and to lobby legislators but was severely disappointed when the bill didn't pass.

''How can I make them understand what this does to young people like me?'' she asks. ``I love school. I want to be a pediatrician. I want to be able to go to school and take classes. I will have a much brighter future.''

MENIAL JOBS

Priya Sampath, policy director for the Human Services Coalition, a nonprofit organization that promotes civic participation and access to health and human services, notes that the current law means that bright immigrant students, who might otherwise become professionals, will have to settle for low-paying menial jobs. Florida taxpayers pay about 75 percent of the cost of educating in-state students, but advocates note that undocumented immigrants pay the same taxes to fund education that all residents do.

''The cost [to the community] is tremendous because of the loss in manpower that can eventually contribute to the community,'' Sampath says.

A report for the coalition entitled Opening the Door to Florida Immigrant College Students cites several studies to back the group's claims, including a RAND Institute analysis that found that Hispanics with a bachelor's degree will pay more that twice as much in taxes during their working life as those with only a high school diploma.

Despite his academic credentials, Matias isn't sure what he will do after graduation if the law doesn't pass. Maybe try to find work, he says, but anything available to a person without proper work documents would probably be menial and low-paying. He hopes that one day his legal status will be settled.

''If given the opportunity, I know I will do well,'' he says. ``I just need the opportunity.''

Proponents of paper voting trail win ruling

        A judge says Sarasota County voters have a right to decide Nov.
7 whether to switch from touch screen to paper ballots.

By ALISA ULFERTS, Times Staff Writer
Published September 14, 2006

  _____ 

A controversial charter amendment that would resurrect the paper ballot
in Sarasota County must be placed on the Nov. 7 ballot, a judge ruled
Wednesday.

The amendment, drafted by a group that distrusts the electronic, touch
screen machines used by Sarasota and 14 other counties - including
Pinellas, Hillsborough and Pasco - is constitutional and has met all
ballot requirements, Circuit Judge Robert B. Bennett Jr. said in his
ruling.

County commissioners, who feared the measure was unconstitutional and
sought a judge's opinion, relented and voted Wednesday afternoon to
place the measure on the general election ballot.

The decision was hailed by paper trail supporters as a victory for
democracy and a needed shot in the arm to other groups around the state
agitating for a paper voting trail.

"This is a great day for the voters of Sarasota County," said Kindra
Muntz, chairwoman of the Sarasota Alliance for Fair Elections. Muntz's
group drafted the proposed amendment and collected the required number
of signatures to get it on the ballot. "This is for all voters of all
parties or no party," Muntz said.

The judge's decision, and the County Commission's vote, cap months of
tension between county officials and SAFE.

For Muntz and other members of SAFE, the issue was simple: No one could
guarantee, to their satisfaction, that the touch screen voting machines
the county purchased could not be rigged.

So SAFE began collecting signatures to ask the county to use a machine
such as the optical scanner, in which voters receive a paper ballot and
a marker to record their votes. Once the ballot is completed, the paper
is run through a scanner that checks for irregularities and then
deposits the ballot in a locked box. SAFE also wants random audits of
the machine results.

They got enough signatures and submitted them to Supervisor of Elections
Kathy Dent, who certified their authenticity.

County commissioners refused to act. Instead, they sued SAFE late last
month and asked a judge to rule on the constitutionality of the issue.

They said the county could lose federal election funds if it placed the
matter before voters because the state hasn't certified any machines
that meet all of SAFE's demands and are accessible to disabled voters.

Judge Bennett said that wasn't reason to keep the amendment off the
ballot because the state could approve such a voting machine for
counties to use in the future.

SAFE isn't the only group trying to switch from a touch screen voting
system back to a voter-verified paper ballot system. A group of citizens
in Broward County also is trying to persuade county commissioners there
to place the question on the Nov. 7 ballot, said group organizer Ellen
Brodsky.

And the Election Reform Coalition of Pinellas County, which comprises
several political organizations, considers getting a paper trail in
Pinellas County one of its top priorities. The coalition is on hiatus
while its members work on other campaigns and elections issues, but
plans to regroup after the election, organizers say.

Don't Limit Education Options For Urban Students
            ADVERTISERS

John G. Rowland

March 12 2004

At an equal opportunity scholarship rally March 4 at the state Capitol,
mothers and fathers and children spoke with eloquence and fervor about
the importance of choosing the right schools, public and private. In
their expressions of support for my proposal to provide financial
assistance to urban families choosing nonpublic schools, one parent put
it best: "As the primary advocates for our daughters' well-being, we as
parents have the responsibility to choose for them the best possible
education."

The great shame is that amid Connecticut's extraordinary system of
public education - better than anywhere in the nation by almost every
standard - we have been content to limit options for parents and
students who may find alternative educational settings and approaches
more appropriate and effective in meeting their needs.

The great shame is that we have tolerated a political culture so timid
about the notion that the public school system may not be right for
every child that we unleash wild exaggerations at the idea of offering a
few kids a ticket to possible success in private or religious schools.

We have credible research now from school choice programs in Milwaukee,
Cleveland and Florida to counter virtually every over-excited criticism
that you will hear of our scholarship program in Connecticut. No, these
programs do not cripple the public school systems; no, these programs do
not cherry-pick only the best students; yes, the students who choose to
move usually do as well as, and often better than, their classmates who
remain in the public schools.

In my program, most of the $4,000 cost of the scholarship would come
from state funds, not the local school district. In fact, the districts
targeted for choice experiments would receive additional money aimed at
improving the failing schools.

There are some of us who have spent more than a decade engaged in debate
about the virtues of these choice programs. It has been an interesting
debate, but the delay has contributed to urban families having to face
failure and frustration rather than freedom and high achievement.

The honest answer: We do have school choice in Connecticut. Motivated
parents with sufficient financial resources make the choice about
schools by selecting an appropriate address. Those families without the
ways and means to do that deserve other options, including private and
religious schools.

For years now, we've disappointed families who see such scholarship
plans implemented across the country while our legislation is quietly
killed, often without even a public hearing.

Now is the time to dispense with the fiction that choice is some
radical, foreign, extreme changing of the public-policy guard in
education. A generation of World War II veterans was unleashed on the
nation's colleges and universities through the GI Bill without regard to
the distinction between "public" and "private" and "religious"
institutions, much like the federal Pell Grant works today. The same
goes for our state's widely touted school readiness program, which
permits parents to choose from programs offered by the Salvation Army,
YMCA or a range of public entities.

What's more, Connecticut has established a vigorous system of public
school choice through magnet schools, charter schools, vo-ags and
vo-techs, and voluntary transfers among public school districts. Several
rural school districts in Connecticut offer their students choices among
several schools in adjoining towns without undue angst or concern.

In housing, through various social-service functions and in many other
government delivery systems, choice is the successful vehicle through
which clients navigate the public and private and faith-based agencies
that deliver the goods. Families deserve the same creative alternatives
in education.

I am proposing a limited experiment, with 500 kids. I know we can
continue our commitment to improving the public school status quo and at
the same time give families throughout the state the immediate option of
trying something different.

John G. Rowland is governor of Connecticut.

With the last day of the 1999 session of the Florida Legislature set for April 30, there are only 3 weeks left to conclude business in Tallahassee. With the blessing of the House leadership, a Senior Caucus has been established to look at issues facing the older citizens of the state.  The group will be looking at legislation to see how it will affect a population that now makes up approximately one-third of the states population - those over 60.  Several meetings have been held and ideas and issues are being gathered.  I recommended we do more to assist older citizens to find enjoyable and gainful employment. At the Tourism Committee meeting Wednesday, April 7, I was amazed at the figures presented relative to the sport of bowling.  The report shows that over 54 million people bowl on a regular basis and there are over 4.5 million regular league bowlers.  For every golfer, there estimated to be two bowlers.  We passed a bill out of committee that will assist Osceola County (south of Orlando) to create the World Bowling Village.  The facility will include a stadium, a national training center, a research and development center and a national headquarters for Bowling, Inc.  It will have a 60-lane stadium that seats 2,000 spectators. The study presented to the committee shows that the project will generate 300 jobs directly, with an average income of $40,000, and 700 or more jobs indirectly in the support industries.  It will also attract over 200,000 visitors to Florida who would otherwise be attending tournaments held elsewhere. If youre a bowler, this is surely good news.  The bill still has to pass the House and Senate before becoming law.  What do you think of this proposed development? Comments: <mailto:jmelvin@gulf1.com>

Last week the House passed HB 295 that would allow insured to elect a deductible amount in combination with the exclusion of wage loss benefits under personal injury protection coverage that is required by Florida law for motor vehicle owners.  Insured would also receive a premium reduction that would be associated with that election of coverage. The bill also provides that an insurer must provide to the insured offers of modification of coverage in a clear and unambiguous written form.  This bill will offer some options to such insurance if it becomes law.

The House also passed HB 229 last week.  It provides that a U.S. Citizen who is not a resident of Florida may carry a concealed weapon or firearm in this state, provided the person is 21 years of age or older and has a valid concealed weapons license from his or her state of residence.  The bill further provides that when the holder of a valid concealed weapons license from another state establishes legal residence in the state of Florida, the license from the previous state remains in effect in Florida for a period of 90 days.  It also limits the applicability of these provisions only to those states which have reciprocity with the state of Florida with respect to the issuance of a concealed weapon or concealed firearms permit. The following article was in Friday's "CongressDaily" regarding the federal
election reform bill, which is currently in Conference Committee between the
House and Senate.  There is a great deal of pressure on the Committee to
finish the bill quickly and a deal is likely in the next few weeks.

There are three provisions mentioned in the article below.  Following is an
update on those provisions:

1.  Poll Worker Training Funds--Both bills authorize funds for training poll
workers.  If the bill is completed this year, Florida would benefit from
funds disbursed during the fiscal year that starts tomorrow.

2.  Timelines--Both bills have very strict timelines for carrying out the
reforms.  Since Congress has delayed in passing the bill, many states have
voiced their concern that there will not be enough time to institute the
reforms before the 2004 election.  We voiced similar concerns to Conference
Committee staff during a conference call in July.

3.  State Database/ID Requirement--It is highly likely that the compromise
bill will include requirements for state-wide databases and identification
checks at polling places.  Most states are very concerned about this
requirement, since only five states have a database already in place.
(Florida has a database system.)

Thanks, Melissa

LOOKING IN
Preventing Future Floridas
     Prompted by Florida's disastrous primary Sept. 10, lawmakers on Capitol
Hill are scrambling to reach final agreement on a sweeping overhaul of the
nation's voting system.
     Florida's recent troubles have prompted House members to press for
quick action on long-stalled election reform legislation. The legislation
passed the House in December and won Senate approval in April but has been
stalemated in conference for months. At the instigation of Rep. Maxine
Waters, D-Calif., the House has now instructed conferees to reconcile the
two bills by Oct. 1 - next Tuesday.
     The rush to finally enact a bill is understandable. After all, two
years have passed since polling problems in Florida disrupted the
presidential election and revealed a nationwide voting system badly in need
of repair. Yet Florida's latest election fiasco suggests that hastily
enacted reforms have a tendency to backfire. The real lesson from Florida
may be: Proceed with caution.
     Florida officials invested $32 million in new voting systems and
equipment, but last month voters faced long lines, uncounted ballots and a
weeklong recount. (In the hotly contested Democratic gubernatorial primary,
former Attorney General Reno eventually conceded to lawyer Bill McBride.)
The problems, according to a recent report: poorly trained precinct clerks
and confusion over new provisional ballots and touch-screen machines.
     "To say to states: 'We'll give you a little money for a new piece of
equipment,' and to throw it on their doorstep with no training resources
would be a major mistake," said Cathy Cox, the Georgia secretary of state
and chairwoman of the elections committee for the National Association of
Secretaries of State.
     Cox and other secretaries of state are eager for a bill, but they worry
that certain provisions now on the table will cause Florida-style problems
nationwide. Both the House and Senate bills set aside $3.5 billion over five
years to help states buy new equipment, upgrade election systems and
establish minimum standards for provisional voting and statewide
registration systems.
     But state officials fear that they will not receive federal funding
quickly enough to make improvements by 2004. It is not clear how much money
will actually be appropriated for FY03, yet the legislation requires certain
minimum standards to be in place before the next election.
     "It's going to be a nightmare if they pass this with unfunded
mandates," said Kay Albowicz, communications director of the National
Association of Secretaries of State. "If they don't put the money in, expect
more Floridas to follow."
     Even more controversial is the Senate bill's requirement that voters
who register by mail bring some form of identification to the polls, such as
a driver's license or utility bill. Sen. Christopher (Kit) Bond, R-Mo., has
argued that the ID provision is a much-needed deterrent to fraud. It has
raised some concerns in the House but appears certain to end up in the final
bill. "There will not be a bill if this provision is out," said an aide to
Bond.
     The ID provision has alarmed civil rights and public interest groups,
who warn it smacks of discrimination and may result in a bill that does more
harm than good. "We certainly need to do this now, but we also need to do it
right," said Adam Lioz, democracy advocate for the U.S. Public Interest
Research Group.
     The provision also raises practical concerns, particularly for the
secretaries of state. They argue that federal ID requirements should be
imposed only on states that already have a centralized, statewide
voter-registration database in place. Only five states have such databases
up and running at the moment. Said Cox of Georgia: "You've kind of got to
get the cart before the horse."
     Yet the proposal now on the table would require states to have voter ID
systems in place by 2004. That is awfully short notice for such a dramatic
change, warned Lloyd Leonard, legislative director of the League of Women
Voters. "If Florida demonstrates anything, it's that it takes a while, it
takes some practice, to get things right," he said. "And so, we are deeply
concerned that the ID requirement, with its early deadline, is going to lead
to confusion in the presidential election."
     Bond does not see why the requirement is such a problem. "They've got
to ask for identification," he said. "How tough is that? It's not rocket
science." Bond also assured that the states would get the money they need,
saying, "We're not going to pass an unfunded mandate." But he acknowledged
that wrestling with the bill's details has proved a challenge. "The devil is
in the drafting," he added.
     If the recent Florida primary proves anything, it is that details
count. Sweeping reforms may do little good if state officials lack the tools
to implement them. "The details are mind-numbing and boring, but they are
absolutely essential," noted Leonard. "And if you get the details wrong,
you're going to have Florida all over again." By Eliza Newlin Carney

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

From: State Representative Jerry Melvin Sent: Monday, March 12, 2001 8:19 AM To: jeb@jeb.org Subject: Fourth Dimension Report for 03/09/01 March 9, 2001 JUDICIAL REFORM ON ITS WAY Many of you know that since my election to the House in 1994, I have constantly been calling for restraints on the Judiciary and the Florida Bar. As the following will show, others are not begining to see what I have been talking about. What do you think? An open letter from Rep. Cantens regarding Judicial Reform There has been a great deal of publicity in recent months about concerns many legislators have with Florida's runaway judicial system. Examples abound of a judiciary that has, in my opinion, overstepped its bounds. As chairman of the Florida House of Representatives Council for Smarter Government, it has been handed to my committee to look for ways to make the judicial branch of our state government more accountable to Florida's citizens. This is not easy. And it has become controversial because many of the state's lawyers enjoy the closed shop that defines our judiciary today. You may near from some of those groups that this is simply a political battle. They will suggest that Republican legislative leaders are simply disturbed by the Florida Supreme Court's decisions during the recent wrangling over the presidential recount. Nonsense. Our concern with the actions of the judicial branch date back long before that significant case. The citizens of the State of Florida established the present constitutional structure of the judiciary in 1972. It sets up an extreme form of judicial independence that has proven to cause difficulties, especially as it restrains and stifles popular government. In 1956, Floridians granted our Supreme Court the power to make procedural rules governing the courts. In 1960, the Florida Supreme Court held unanimously that its rule-making power could not alter the substantive rights of anyone. It remained to the Legislature, or the people through their constitution, to regulate substantive rights. Last year, however, in striking down the Death Penalty Reform Act, passed by a bi-partisan two-thirds of the people's elected representatives, the court went to the other extreme, holding that substantive laws passed by the representatives of the people must yield to procedural rules of the court. By this device, courts could refuse to enforce any law enacted by the Legislature. Imagine how destructive that would be to our representative form of government. -more- Under our republican form of government, decisions of our highest court must be respected. To change the effect of unpopular judicial decisions we must change laws or constitutional provisions. Our founders intended to make this difficult, to insure that people would engage in serious deliberation and reflection, rather than mere reactionary tactics, to overrule the independent judiciary. The founders rejected any notion of the other government branches vetoing judicial decisions. But the right and power of the people to do so, by constitutional amendment if necessary, was paramount, and never forbidden - until now. In Florida, the ability of the people to overrule the courts, and exercise their ultimate authority to govern themselves by amending their own constitution has been drastically undermined by the Florida Supreme Court. Last September, the court ruled the constitution itself unconstitutional, upon a principle it suddenly found to be hidden, i.e., implicit, in the constitution. The Legislature unanimously put an amendment to preserve the death penalty on the ballot in 1998. The people voted overwhelmingly to adopt that amendment. But 22 months after the election, the court said the ballot was insufficient and nullified the votes of millions of Floridians. This decision was so extreme that the Florida Attorney General is appealing to the United States Supreme Court. The Attorney General's office has asked the nation's highest court to rule that our state court has trampled the fundamental and most sacred right of Florida voters to govern themselves. These are but two circumstances indicating that the pendulum between judicial independence and popular self-government has swung too far and that our judiciary is out of control. Every generation can and should examine our constitutional separation of powers and make adjustments as necessary. If the people want the courts to decide for them what questions may be addressed through legislation and direct voting on constitutional amendments, the people can so choose. But if today's Floridians wish to govern themselves, and undertake the difficult responsibility of self-determination that so many of our forebears have suffered and died to win for us, we must look carefully at the present situation, and consider changes. Should procedural rules adopted by unelected judges overrule laws passed by the Legislature? Should judges be able to strike constitutional provisions based upon their subjective determination that you as a voter were too ignorant to vote on the amendment? Should the Florida Governor be limited to choosing judges only from lists approved by appointees of the unelected, unrepresentative Florida Bar Association? Should all judges be popularly elected? Should the Florida Bar continue to exercise the sole government power to regulate lawyers, insulating them from the reach of the people's elected representative? These are all questions worth asking. There are many strong arguments for and against the possible answers to these questions. In fact, many of these questions have already been asked and answered by our Federal judicial system. Many of the proposals being discussed and debated in Tallahassee this spring would conform our state balance of powers to the Federal system. The President of the United States nominates judges to the Federal courts, subject to confirmation by the United States Senate, without need for control by any committees or nominating commissions. That process works to keep balance in our federal courts. Federal judges are the best and most qualified judges in the country. -more - In contrast, Florida has a system of nominating commissions that screen all applicants and then submit three to six names to the Governor for consideration. Thus, limiting the choices available to Florida's Governor. Taken to an extreme, if all seven Florida Supreme Court seats were to be vacant simultaneously, the Governor would have to choose seven justices from amongst no more than 42 lawyers nominated by the commission. The Governor would have no opportunity to determine whether any of the other thousands of lawyers and judges in the State might be equally qualified. As another example, the U.S. Congress promulgates the Federal Rules of Procedure with input from the Federal courts. In Florida, however, the courts promulgate rules of procedure to the exclusion of the legislative bodies. There are no checks and balances. Lawyers and Judges should and must be zealous defenders of individual liberties. But ultimately, the people, through their own constitution and their own elected representatives and executives, must hold the authority to define those liberties. Otherwise, we will cease to be self-governed. Your state legislators are the policy makers chosen by you to represent you and your views. As we debate this incredibly important issue this legislative session, I encourage each of you to share your opinions with your Representative or Senator. That is what makes your government work. From:	Muniz, Carlos <Carlos.Muniz@MyFlorida.com>
Sent:	Wednesday, September 25, 2002 7:21 PM
To:	Jeb Bush; Shanahan, Kathleen
Cc:	Canady, Charles T.; Muniz, Katie
Subject:	Voter List Issues

A law enacted in 1998--but since repealed by the Election Reform Act of
2001--required the Division of Elections to contract with a private entity
to compile a list of registered voters who were (1) deceased, (2)
adjudicated as mentally incompetent, or (3) felons without restoration of
civil rights.  (For simplicity, I'll refer to this as the "felon list".)
The law further directed the Division of Elections to distribute that list
to the supervisors of elections, so that they could use the list to
update/clean up their voter registration rolls.  The firm ultimately hired
by the Division of Elections was Database Technologies, Inc., a subsidiary
of ChoicePoint, Inc.

In the wake of the 2000 election, the felon list became a matter of great
controversy.  Some of the more incendiary press accounts claimed that
"thousands" of potential voters had been wrongly "purged" from the voter
rolls.  However, a comprehensive study by the Palm Beach Post yielded an
estimate of 1,104 persons wrongly removed from the voter rolls.  The Palm
Beach Post also reported that 20 of the 67 supervisors of elections
(including those in Broward and Palm Beach counties) did not use the felon
list at all.  (To put the matter in further context: the same Palm Beach
Post study concluded that approximately 5,600 felons voted (illegally) in
the November 2000 election.)  To my knowledge, there has been no independent
inquiry by the state as to how many voters were wrongly removed from the
voting rolls as a result of the felon list.  
  
The Election Reform Act of 2001 repealed the requirement that the Division
of Elections hire a private firm to compile the felon list.  The law now
requires the Division of Elections to perform that function in-house.  The
law also now gives the supervisors of elections detailed guidelines as to
the notice and opportunity to be heard that they must give persons
identified as potential felons.

Substantively, the most significant changes between the old and new list
compilation procedures are as follows:  

1.  The new list relies only on data provided by FDLE, which data includes
only Florida convictions and which the Division of Elections believes is the
most accurate available.  The old list included data from the Department of
Corrections and from other states.  Using data from other states was a
problem because there is no uniformity among states with regard to clemency
rules.

2.  The new list uses much stricter "matching criteria" for identifying
potential felons whose civil rights are unrestored.  I can give you a
summary of those criteria at your request.

Finally, there is the matter of the settlement agreement finalized on
September 12, 2002 between the NAACP and the Division of Elections.  That
agreement requires the Division to re-examine the felon lists created prior
to the 2000 election and to provide supervisors of elections with the names
of persons who were on those lists, but who do not meet the current matching
criteria.  The supervisors must then use that information to verify whether
anyone was improperly removed from the voter rolls because of the old felon
lists.  Significantly, the NAACP has implicitly endorsed the validity of the
matching criteria that have been developed by the Division of Elections.

In the settlement agreement, the NAACP agreed that the Division of Elections
would not perform the list comparison until after the November 2002
election.  In any event, even without that provision, DOJ's requirement that
the settlement agreement be precleared makes it unlikely that the comparison
and subsequent follow-up could be completed before this year's election.

The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values. Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Some of the key points we discussed included: 

*	Timing of the legislative authorization to implement the waiver.  They were thinking next regular session.  We argued for earlier, preferably immediately after receiving the waiver.
*	Contents of the legislation. They were proposing a minimalist first step with enactment of most of the details postponed until the implementing legislation. *	Senior Health Choices.  We both agree that the legislation should authorize implementation of the plan for integrated long term care; however, they want the program to be voluntary and we recommend mandatory enrollment in managed care with assurances regarding access/use of nursing homes.
*	Two-pronged approach.  We both agree that the legislation can initiate the comprehensive reform and make certain changes/enhancements to the existing program.

From:	christinamcalpin@yahoo.com
Sent:	Friday, June 25, 2004 3:47 AM
To:	Jeb Bush
Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Bush,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Maria McAlpin 3025 Broadway, #4 Boulder, CO 80304 United States

-----Original Message-----
From: Arthur Palamara [mailto:aepal@bellsouth.net]
Sent: Tuesday, April 22, 2003 1:04 AM
To: Linda Quick
Cc: bcma1
Subject: impending crisis

Linda:
You would be well served to advise the members of the SFHHA to prepare
contingency plans in the event of a medical liability crisis that will
likely force physicians to curtail their services in early May.
 
My sources tell me that many of the large group practices have already been
in contact with their insurers and are facing extraordinary premium
increases July 1st.  They are also frustrated that the legislature has
failed to act despite overwhelming evidence that indicates that the
recommendations of the Blue Ribbon Committee would substantially reduce
premiums.
 
Most of the doctor have confided in me that they will be forced to limit
high risk services or stop practice entirely.  It is curious that the Miami
Herald editorial two weeks ago stated that 6% of the doctors are responsible
for 51% of the awards yet those 6% actually represent a cross section of
physicians - neurosurgeons, vascular, cardiac, general surgeons,
radiologists obstetricians and ER doctors - who practice high risk
specialties.
 
I surmise that many other practitioners will follow suit both in sympathy
and frustration.
 
It is incumbent on the hospital administrators to notify their regional
Departments of Health well in advance to establish a response plan.  I
anticipate that the District Health Departments will want to notify Dr. John
Aguanobi, Secretary of Heath, to enable him to insure that a alternative
network is in place.
 
From my personal perspective, it is vitally important to protect the public
and make sure that all emergencies are treated.  While the public will
suffer some inconvenience, it would be tragic were someone to die because of
the senate's failure to act.
 
Arthur E. Palamara, MD

Dear Governor Bush:

   As an attorney practicing in the Tampa Bay area for the past nine years,
with four years almost exclusively in the field of adoption, I would like to
voice my objections to SB 138.  I am vigorously opposed to the adoption
bill.  Florida has a good adoption law currently and these extensive,
oppressive changes will dramatically increase abortions and the placement of
children in state foster care.  There are several inconsistencies in the
proposed legislation.  Additionally, the legislation will have a detrimental
effect on the ability of birth mothers to place their children for adoption
while also making it a more expensive and more frightening prospect for
adoptive parents.

  Examples of inconsistencies include:

 - Proving a 48 hr. waiting period for a hospitalized birth mother with no
revocation period yet then including language in the consent regarding
revoking "1 business day after the date of the birth mother's discharge from
a licensed hospital or birth center".

 - Requiring fraud or duress to invalidate a consent (after signing if a
hospitalized birth mother but after 3 days/placement with adoptive parents
if a non-hospitalized birth mother), but then subsequently allowing a birth
mother to object to the placement of the child for "good cause".

 - It is unclear why birth mothers have different rights in different
situations, i.e. placement of newborn vs. placement of child slightly older.
These provisions raise constitutional questions.

 - Under the definition of abandonment , a court may declare a child to be
abandoned if the parent makes only marginal efforts to support and
communicate with a child "that do not evince a settled purpose to assume all
parental duties".  However, a birth father is required to consent if the
birth father "has attempted to provide the child or the mother during her
pregnancy with support in a repetitive, customary manner".  How is the court
to realistically determine whether or not a birth father "attempted to
provide support" in a repetitive manner?  Is this a case of his word "I
tried to call you" against her word "he knew I couldn't pay rent and refused
to help me."  The uncertainty that this raises will be very difficult on a
birth mother.

  - Providing for a waiver of venue by a birth parent  but then allowing
that birth parent to object to venue at a later date.  The waiver thus has
no legal effect.  (Additionally, the venue change will drastically increase
the adoptive parents cost of the adoption because it will require additional
filing fees, attorney involvement, etc.)

  Difficulties for birth mother:

  - In attempting to protect the birth father's rights, the legislation
makes it very unclear to a birth mother whether her adoption plan will be
upheld.  For instance,  a birth father who claims not to be the father or
who plans not to raise paternity cannot sign before birth.  Thus, the birth
mother has no assurance from the man who denies paternity that he will be
around to sign after birth or will cooperate with her adoption plan.

  -  Additionally, the legislation broadens the definition of a "parent" who
must consent to include "any person" who is a party in any paternity,
custody or termination proceeding.    Are these persons grandparents (who in
another section have rights only if the child lived with them for 6 months),
aunts, uncles, etc.?

  -  The obligation is fully on the birth mother to notify the birth father
and demand support while the birth father appears to have a right to object
by just receiving a positive paternity test after birth.  Is no support
required pre-birth in this instance?  How and when will a birth mother know
whether she has the support of the birth father?  Many times women choose
abortion because a birth father tells them he is planning to contest the
adoption when he has a paternity test determining he's the father.
Paternity testing occurs well after the mother has had a dire need for
support, made her decision to provide a loving home for the child, met the
prospective adoptive family and had the baby.

  -  A putative birth father registry is the best way to protect everyone's
rights - birth mother, birth father, adoptive parents.  36 other states have
enacted birth father registries.

  - Can the birth mother even understand her revocation rights the way they
are currently written?  There are too many ifs, ands or buts in the language
of the required consent document.  This will increase rather than decrease
litigation.

  The adoptive parents plight:

  - The child can be placed in their home pending termination of parental
rights yet the parent can question the placement (as mentioned above) even
after signing consents.

  - The court order approving the placement occurs subsequent to placement.

  - The birth father appears to be able to object at any time up to two
years with the possibility that he may not have been required to support the
birth mother.  His best recourse seems to be to disappear for the pregnancy
so he cannot be contacted and show up post-birth to object to the adoption.

  - A person whose consent is required may challenge the validity of "any
consent or affidavit of nonpaternity" signed by any other person.   One
potential birth father can challenge another's affidavit of nonpaternity or
even the birth mother's consent?

  - The contesting parent is entititled to fees yet a prevailing adoptive
parent is not.  The adoptive parents requirement to repay the birth parents
fees (if the adoption is overturned but not through an act or omission of
the adoption entity) along with the requirement to file in the venue of each
possible birth father will substantially increase the cost of adoptions.

  These are just some of the problems that exist with the legislation.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
